questions.section: Content Domain 1: Data Preparation for Machine Learning (ML)
questions.question_text:
A regional grocery chain's personalization team maintains several models that use customer loyalty, store inventory, and recent purchase features. Different teams currently recompute the same features in separate notebooks and endpoint containers, which has produced inconsistent feature values between training and real-time recommendations. The team needs reusable feature data, low-latency access for deployed models, and batch access for recurring training jobs over historical records.

Which actions should the team take? (Select TWO.)
questions.question_html: A regional grocery chain's personalization team maintains several models that use customer loyalty, store inventory, and recent purchase features. Different teams currently recompute the same features in separate notebooks and endpoint containers, which has produced inconsistent feature values between training and real-time recommendations. The team needs reusable feature data, low-latency access for deployed models, and batch access for recurring training jobs over historical records. Which actions should the team take? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Register each shared feature set in SageMaker Model Registry as a model package version.
options.B: Create SageMaker Feature Store feature groups with online and offline stores for the shared features.
options.C: Keep independent feature transformation code in each training notebook and endpoint container.
options.D: Store feature values in SageMaker Experiments trials and query the trials during inference.
options.E: Read live feature values from the online store and build training datasets from the offline store.

options_list: Register each shared feature set in SageMaker Model Registry as a model package version.
Create SageMaker Feature Store feature groups with online and offline stores for the shared features.
Keep independent feature transformation code in each training notebook and endpoint container.
Store feature values in SageMaker Experiments trials and query the trials during inference.
Read live feature values from the online store and build training datasets from the offline store.
correct_answers_text: Create SageMaker Feature Store feature groups with online and offline stores for the shared features.
Read live feature values from the online store and build training datasets from the offline store.
questions.explanation_text:
**Amazon SageMaker Feature Store** is intended to make engineered features reusable and consistent across the ML lifecycle. Instead of recomputing customer, store, or transaction features separately for every model, teams create feature groups that define and organize shared feature records.

The key design choice in this scenario is the use of both storage modes. The **online store** supports low-latency feature access for deployed models, while the **offline store** stores historical feature records in Amazon S3 for batch training and analysis. This split exists because inference and training have different access patterns: one needs fast point lookups, while the other usually scans or joins larger historical datasets.

SageMaker Model Registry and SageMaker Experiments are valuable MLOps tools, but they solve different problems. Model Registry manages model versions and approvals, and Experiments tracks development runs and metrics. Neither service is a substitute for a central feature repository.

For more information, see Amazon SageMaker Feature Store and Feature Store storage configurations.

questions.question_text:
A telehealth provider's care coordination team hosts an appointment no-show prediction model on an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint. The team has baseline statistics from the training dataset, and actual attendance labels arrive in Amazon S3 each night. The team needs to receive alerts when live request features drift from the baseline or when prediction quality degrades, with the least custom monitoring code.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
questions.question_html: A telehealth provider's care coordination team hosts an appointment no-show prediction model on an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint. The team has baseline statistics from the training dataset, and actual attendance labels arrive in Amazon S3 each night. The team needs to receive alerts when live request features drift from the baseline or when prediction quality degrades, with the least custom monitoring code. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Run SageMaker Clarify bias drift monitoring on the endpoint, configure CloudWatch alarms, and retrain the model when bias thresholds change.
options.B: Create CloudWatch dashboards for endpoint invocations and latency, configure alarms on high latency, and review application logs after traffic spikes.
options.C: Enable CloudTrail management event logging for SageMaker, store the trail in Amazon S3, and query endpoint API activity with Athena.
options.D: Enable Data Capture on the endpoint, create data quality and model quality monitoring schedules from baselines, and configure CloudWatch alarms on violations.

options_list: Run SageMaker Clarify bias drift monitoring on the endpoint, configure CloudWatch alarms, and retrain the model when bias thresholds change.
Create CloudWatch dashboards for endpoint invocations and latency, configure alarms on high latency, and review application logs after traffic spikes.
Enable CloudTrail management event logging for SageMaker, store the trail in Amazon S3, and query endpoint API activity with Athena.
Enable Data Capture on the endpoint, create data quality and model quality monitoring schedules from baselines, and configure CloudWatch alarms on violations.
correct_answers_text: Enable Data Capture on the endpoint, create data quality and model quality monitoring schedules from baselines, and configure CloudWatch alarms on violations.
questions.explanation_text:
**Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor** is designed for the production monitoring concerns in this scenario. It can monitor data quality drift by comparing live inference data to a baseline, and it can monitor model quality when ground truth labels become available after predictions are made. See the SageMaker overview for the supported monitoring types in Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor.

**Data Capture** is the practical starting point for endpoint monitoring because it records inference inputs and outputs to Amazon S3 for later analysis. Those captured records can be used for monitoring, debugging, and retraining workflows, as described in Capture data from deployed models.

CloudWatch is still part of the solution, but it is not sufficient by itself. CloudWatch endpoint metrics can tell an engineer whether an endpoint is busy, slow, or unhealthy, while Model Monitor emits monitoring results that can be used for alarms when statistical constraints or quality expectations are violated. Data quality monitoring and model quality monitoring are covered in Monitor data quality and Monitor model quality metrics.

CloudTrail and Clarify solve adjacent but different problems. CloudTrail records API activity for audit investigations, and Clarify is appropriate when the requirement is bias drift or feature attribution drift. For this scenario, the best fit is managed monitoring of both live feature distributions and prediction quality, with alerts through CloudWatch.

The pattern includes a source repository, automated build and test stages, Amazon SageMaker processing and training jobs, model evaluation, registration in SageMaker Model Registry, and a separate deployment workflow for approved models. The group wants to script this pattern so new projects can be created consistently with minimal custom orchestration code and traceable CI/CD assets.

Which TWO actions should the ML engineer take?

The pattern includes a source repository, automated build and test stages, Amazon SageMaker processing and training jobs, model evaluation, registration in SageMaker Model Registry, and a separate deployment workflow for approved models. The group wants to script this pattern so new projects can be created consistently with minimal custom orchestration code and traceable CI/CD assets. Which TWO actions should the ML engineer take?

options.A: Create a SageMaker Project from an MLOps template to provision the repository, build, deploy, and workflow resources.
options.B: Create ECS services on Fargate for each ML lifecycle stage and scale the task count for training and deployment.
options.C: Create EventBridge rules for each lifecycle event to invoke separate SageMaker jobs and update deployments independently.
options.D: Define a SageMaker Pipeline for the processing, training, evaluation, and registration stages, and version the definition with the code.
options.E: Create a Step Functions state machine to call SageMaker jobs and manually maintain model promotion logic.

options_list: Create a SageMaker Project from an MLOps template to provision the repository, build, deploy, and workflow resources.
Create ECS services on Fargate for each ML lifecycle stage and scale the task count for training and deployment.
Create EventBridge rules for each lifecycle event to invoke separate SageMaker jobs and update deployments independently.
Define a SageMaker Pipeline for the processing, training, evaluation, and registration stages, and version the definition with the code.
Create a Step Functions state machine to call SageMaker jobs and manually maintain model promotion logic.
correct_answers_text: Create a SageMaker Project from an MLOps template to provision the repository, build, deploy, and workflow resources.
Define a SageMaker Pipeline for the processing, training, evaluation, and registration stages, and version the definition with the code.
questions.explanation_text:
**SageMaker Projects** and **SageMaker Pipelines** work together for this type of requirement. A project template gives a team a repeatable MLOps scaffold, such as repositories and CI/CD resources, while a pipeline defines the actual ML workflow stages that run processing, training, evaluation, and model registration. See SageMaker MLOps project templates and Amazon SageMaker Pipelines.

The important mental model is to separate *project infrastructure* from *workflow orchestration*. Projects standardize how a new ML project is created and governed, while Pipelines captures the repeatable DAG-like ML process that can be versioned, executed, and integrated into CI/CD. EventBridge and Step Functions are useful orchestration tools in many AWS architectures, and Step Functions can call SageMaker jobs as shown in AWS Step Functions integration with SageMaker, but using them as the primary mechanism here would require more custom coordination than the stated requirement calls for. ECS on Fargate is a valid serverless container platform, but it is not the lowest-overhead way to recreate a SageMaker-centered ML lifecycle pattern.

Which solution best meets these requirements?

questions.explanation_text:
**CI/CD in ML** extends normal application delivery practices to include data processing, training, evaluation, model versioning, approval, and deployment. SageMaker Pipelines models the ML workflow as repeatable steps, such as processing, training, evaluation, and model registration. CodePipeline and CodeBuild fit around that workflow by automating source, build, test, and release stages, which gives teams traceability and a safer promotion path from staging to production.

Model Registry alone is not enough because it is primarily a catalog and governance mechanism for model versions, not a complete workflow orchestrator. A custom CodeBuild and EventBridge solution can work for simple automation, but it requires the team to recreate MLOps capabilities that SageMaker Projects and Pipelines already provide. Deploying directly to ECS on Fargate is a valid container pattern for some applications, but it does not meet the stated need to manage SageMaker ML workflow steps with minimal custom orchestration.

questions.question_text:
A public university's research computing team is creating a central repository for genomics CSV files, experiment metadata in JSON, and microscope images. Different labs will use the repository for future analytics and machine learning projects, but the access patterns and final schemas are not yet known. The team wants to minimize initial storage cost and avoid upfront data modeling while keeping the data available for later SQL based exploration.

Which storage approach best meets these requirements?
questions.question_html: A public university's research computing team is creating a central repository for genomics CSV files, experiment metadata in JSON, and microscope images. Different labs will use the repository for future analytics and machine learning projects, but the access patterns and final schemas are not yet known. The team wants to minimize initial storage cost and avoid upfront data modeling while keeping the data available for later SQL based exploration. Which storage approach best meets these requirements?

options.A: Place the data on Amazon EFS, mount the file system from notebooks, and organize the files by lab directory.
options.B: Load the data into Amazon Redshift tables, define the schema before ingestion, and query the data with Redshift SQL.
options.C: Import the data into Amazon FSx for Lustre, process the files from training jobs, and keep the repository on the file system.
options.D: Store the raw data in Amazon S3 as a data lake, catalog the datasets with AWS Glue, and query the data with Amazon Athena.

options_list: Place the data on Amazon EFS, mount the file system from notebooks, and organize the files by lab directory.
Load the data into Amazon Redshift tables, define the schema before ingestion, and query the data with Redshift SQL.
Import the data into Amazon FSx for Lustre, process the files from training jobs, and keep the repository on the file system.
Store the raw data in Amazon S3 as a data lake, catalog the datasets with AWS Glue, and query the data with Amazon Athena.
correct_answers_text: Store the raw data in Amazon S3 as a data lake, catalog the datasets with AWS Glue, and query the data with Amazon Athena.
questions.explanation_text:
When the data includes a mix of **structured**, **semi-structured**, and **unstructured** formats, and the future analytics requirements are uncertain, an **Amazon S3 data lake** is typically the best initial storage decision. A data lake stores raw data in its native format and supports schema-on-read, so teams can defer modeling decisions until they understand how the data will be used.

**AWS Glue** can provide catalog metadata for data stored in S3, and **Amazon Athena** can query that data with SQL without loading it into a warehouse first. This balances cost and flexibility because the team avoids transforming every dataset into a fixed schema before there is a proven analytics need.

A warehouse such as Amazon Redshift is better when the data is already structured and the organization needs fast, repeated, complex BI queries over a known schema. File systems such as Amazon EFS and Amazon FSx for Lustre solve different problems, shared POSIX access and high performance file processing, but they are not the best default repository for a flexible analytics and ML data lake.

For additional context, see the AWS storage decision guide, the Amazon S3 storage classes documentation, and the SageMaker guidance on accessing training data from storage services.
questions.explanation_html:
When the data includes a mix of structured, semi-structured, and unstructured formats, and the future analytics requirements are uncertain, an Amazon S3 data lake is typically the best initial storage decision. A data lake stores raw data in its native format and supports schema-on-read, so teams can defer modeling decisions until they understand how the data will be used.

AWS Glue can provide catalog metadata for data stored in S3, and Amazon Athena can query that data with SQL without loading it into a warehouse first. This balances cost and flexibility because the team avoids transforming every dataset into a fixed schema before there is a proven analytics need.

A warehouse such as Amazon Redshift is better when the data is already structured and the organization needs fast, repeated, complex BI queries over a known schema. File systems such as Amazon EFS and Amazon FSx for Lustre solve different problems, shared POSIX access and high performance file processing, but they are not the best default repository for a flexible analytics and ML data lake.

For additional context, see the AWS storage decision guide, the Amazon S3 storage classes documentation, and the SageMaker guidance on accessing training data from storage services.

questions.question_text:
A property insurance carrier's actuarial ML team is selecting a model to predict claim severity from tabular policy, property, and weather features. Several candidate models meet the minimum RMSE target, but compliance reviewers require the team to understand which features influence predictions before the model is approved. The team wants to include interpretability in the model selection process without abandoning managed SageMaker workflows.

Which TWO actions should the team take?
questions.question_html: A property insurance carrier's actuarial ML team is selecting a model to predict claim severity from tabular policy, property, and weather features. Several candidate models meet the minimum RMSE target, but compliance reviewers require the team to understand which features influence predictions before the model is approved. The team wants to include interpretability in the model selection process without abandoning managed SageMaker workflows. Which TWO actions should the team take?

options.A: Choose the candidate with the lowest RMSE and defer feature contribution analysis until production monitoring begins.
options.B: Select the least complex candidate algorithm that satisfies the predefined performance and explainability requirements.
options.C: Use SageMaker Model Monitor data quality baselines as the primary method to explain each candidate model.
options.D: Compare candidate models by using SageMaker Clarify feature attribution results together with validation metrics.
options.E: Select an ensemble or deep learning model whenever it improves RMSE, regardless of the added model complexity.

options_list: Choose the candidate with the lowest RMSE and defer feature contribution analysis until production monitoring begins.
Select the least complex candidate algorithm that satisfies the predefined performance and explainability requirements.
Use SageMaker Model Monitor data quality baselines as the primary method to explain each candidate model.
Compare candidate models by using SageMaker Clarify feature attribution results together with validation metrics.
Select an ensemble or deep learning model whenever it improves RMSE, regardless of the added model complexity.
correct_answers_text: Select the least complex candidate algorithm that satisfies the predefined performance and explainability requirements.
Compare candidate models by using SageMaker Clarify feature attribution results together with validation metrics.
questions.explanation_text:
Interpretability should be considered *during* model and algorithm selection, not bolted on only after deployment. A practical selection process compares candidate models on the required performance metric, such as RMSE for a regression problem, and also evaluates whether the model behavior can be explained to stakeholders who must approve or use the predictions.

**SageMaker Clarify** helps with this tradeoff by producing feature attribution information, including SHAP-based explanations, so teams can understand how input features contribute to predictions. This is especially useful when comparing a simpler model that barely meets the target against a more complex model with a small performance gain. See Amazon SageMaker Clarify model explainability and Feature attributions that use Shapley values.

A simpler algorithm can be the better engineering choice when it meets the business performance threshold. For example, **Linear Learner** learns a linear function or linear threshold function for regression and classification, which can be easier to reason about than a large ensemble or deep neural network. The point is not that simple models are always best, but that *accuracy versus complexity* is a real model development tradeoff. See SageMaker Linear Learner algorithm.

Production monitoring and model governance artifacts are still useful later in the lifecycle, but they do not replace interpretability analysis when selecting a candidate model. If a team chooses the lowest-RMSE model without checking feature contribution and explanation quality, it can end up with a model that is difficult to audit, debug, or justify even though it performs well on validation data.

questions.section: Content Domain 1: Data Preparation for Machine Learning (ML)
questions.question_text:
An online education platform's learner analytics team stores raw enrollment and support-ticket exports as CSV files in Amazon S3. The team must determine which datasets contain personally identifiable information (PII) and create a sanitized S3 output for model development. Analysts need repeatable visual preparation steps that can mask, hash, or delete PII fields without writing custom code.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
questions.question_html: An online education platform's learner analytics team stores raw enrollment and support-ticket exports as CSV files in Amazon S3. The team must determine which datasets contain personally identifiable information (PII) and create a sanitized S3 output for model development. Analysts need repeatable visual preparation steps that can mask, hash, or delete PII fields without writing custom code. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.A: Use AWS Lake Formation LF-Tags to classify PII columns. Grant analysts data filters that hide sensitive columns when querying catalog tables.
options.B: Use Amazon Comprehend to detect PII entities in the CSV files. Redact the original files in place before analysts run data preparation jobs.
options.C: Use Amazon Macie to discover sensitive data in S3. Use AWS Glue DataBrew profile and recipe jobs to apply PII transformations and write sanitized data to S3.
options.D: Enable AWS KMS encryption on the S3 bucket. Grant analysts access to the KMS key and require SageMaker jobs to read encrypted raw objects.

options_list: Use AWS Lake Formation LF-Tags to classify PII columns. Grant analysts data filters that hide sensitive columns when querying catalog tables.
Use Amazon Comprehend to detect PII entities in the CSV files. Redact the original files in place before analysts run data preparation jobs.
Use Amazon Macie to discover sensitive data in S3. Use AWS Glue DataBrew profile and recipe jobs to apply PII transformations and write sanitized data to S3.
Enable AWS KMS encryption on the S3 bucket. Grant analysts access to the KMS key and require SageMaker jobs to read encrypted raw objects.
correct_answers_text: Use Amazon Macie to discover sensitive data in S3. Use AWS Glue DataBrew profile and recipe jobs to apply PII transformations and write sanitized data to S3.
questions.explanation_text:
**Amazon Macie** is designed to discover and classify sensitive data in Amazon S3, which makes it a good first step when a team needs to understand where PII exists across data lake objects. Macie helps identify sensitive data so the team can make informed decisions about which datasets need additional controls or transformation before they are used for ML.

**AWS Glue DataBrew** is a visual data preparation tool that supports PII identification and obfuscation-oriented transformations. For this scenario, a DataBrew profile job can help inspect the dataset, and a recipe job can apply actions such as masking, hashing, substitution, encryption, nulling, or deletion before writing a sanitized output to S3.

Encryption with KMS is important for protecting data, but it is not the same as anonymization or masking. Lake Formation permissions and filters are useful for governing access to cataloged data, but access control alone does not produce a reusable de-identified training dataset. Comprehend can be useful for PII detection and redaction in text, but DataBrew is the better fit when analysts need a visual, repeatable preparation workflow for tabular files.

For more information, see Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery in S3, AWS Glue DataBrew personal information protection, and AWS Lake Formation data filters.

questions.question_text:
A live music ticketing platform's ML data engineering team receives two real-time event feeds. The purchase feed only needs lightweight per-record normalization before delivery to Amazon S3 for a training data lake, and the team does not need to replay that feed. The behavioral feed requires continuous cleansing, windowed aggregation, and enrichment by using Spark before loading curated records for downstream ML. The team wants managed AWS services and minimal custom infrastructure.

Which TWO actions will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
questions.question_html: A live music ticketing platform's ML data engineering team receives two real-time event feeds. The purchase feed only needs lightweight per-record normalization before delivery to Amazon S3 for a training data lake, and the team does not need to replay that feed. The behavioral feed requires continuous cleansing, windowed aggregation, and enrichment by using Spark before loading curated records for downstream ML. The team wants managed AWS services and minimal custom infrastructure. Which TWO actions will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Configure Amazon Data Firehose as the replayable stream buffer and run downstream transformations after rereading retained events.
options.B: Query incoming events with Amazon Athena workgroups and schedule CTAS statements to transform each stream into curated S3 files.
options.C: Create an AWS Glue streaming ETL job to consume the behavioral stream and run Spark transformations before writing curated output.
options.D: Build a SageMaker Data Wrangler flow with Quick Model and use the flow as the continuous processor for both streams.
options.E: Configure Amazon Data Firehose to invoke AWS Lambda for lightweight purchase record normalization before delivering events to Amazon S3.

options_list: Configure Amazon Data Firehose as the replayable stream buffer and run downstream transformations after rereading retained events.
Query incoming events with Amazon Athena workgroups and schedule CTAS statements to transform each stream into curated S3 files.
Create an AWS Glue streaming ETL job to consume the behavioral stream and run Spark transformations before writing curated output.
Build a SageMaker Data Wrangler flow with Quick Model and use the flow as the continuous processor for both streams.
Configure Amazon Data Firehose to invoke AWS Lambda for lightweight purchase record normalization before delivering events to Amazon S3.
correct_answers_text: Create an AWS Glue streaming ETL job to consume the behavioral stream and run Spark transformations before writing curated output.
Configure Amazon Data Firehose to invoke AWS Lambda for lightweight purchase record normalization before delivering events to Amazon S3.
questions.explanation_text:
**Amazon Data Firehose** is a good fit when the goal is to load streaming data into a destination such as Amazon S3 with low operational overhead. It can buffer records and invoke **AWS Lambda** to transform incoming data before delivery, which makes it suitable for lightweight normalization such as reshaping records or converting formats. See Transform source data in Amazon Data Firehose.

For the behavioral feed, the requirement is not just per-record transformation. Continuous cleansing, enrichment, and windowed aggregation are classic streaming ETL tasks, and **AWS Glue streaming ETL** uses Spark-based processing patterns for this kind of managed transformation workload. The relevant documentation pages are Adding streaming ETL jobs in AWS Glue and AWS Glue streaming concepts.

**Athena** is excellent for SQL analysis over data in Amazon S3, especially with formats such as Parquet, but it is not a streaming transformation engine. **SageMaker Data Wrangler** helps ML teams visually prepare, profile, and transform data, but it is not the runtime for always-on stream processing. Firehose also should not be treated as a replayable stream buffer, because its role is managed delivery rather than durable stream retention and replay.

questions.question_text:
A pharmaceutical clinical operations team hosts an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint that predicts whether clinical trial sites will miss enrollment targets. After the team launches a new patient referral channel, engineers want alerts if production request features begin to differ statistically from the training baseline. Outcome labels are delayed by several months, and the team wants a managed approach with minimal custom code.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
questions.question_html: A pharmaceutical clinical operations team hosts an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint that predicts whether clinical trial sites will miss enrollment targets. After the team launches a new patient referral channel, engineers want alerts if production request features begin to differ statistically from the training baseline. Outcome labels are delayed by several months, and the team wants a managed approach with minimal custom code. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Enable SageMaker Model Monitor model quality monitoring, configure ground truth label ingestion, and alarm on accuracy metric deviations.
options.B: Enable CloudTrail Insights for SageMaker management events, route insights to EventBridge, and alarm on endpoint update anomalies.
options.C: Enable SageMaker Clarify bias drift monitoring, configure referral channel as a facet, and alarm on bias metric thresholds.
options.D: Enable SageMaker Model Monitor data quality monitoring, create a training-data baseline, and configure CloudWatch alarms for constraint violations.

options_list: Enable SageMaker Model Monitor model quality monitoring, configure ground truth label ingestion, and alarm on accuracy metric deviations.
Enable CloudTrail Insights for SageMaker management events, route insights to EventBridge, and alarm on endpoint update anomalies.
Enable SageMaker Clarify bias drift monitoring, configure referral channel as a facet, and alarm on bias metric thresholds.
Enable SageMaker Model Monitor data quality monitoring, create a training-data baseline, and configure CloudWatch alarms for constraint violations.
correct_answers_text: Enable SageMaker Model Monitor data quality monitoring, create a training-data baseline, and configure CloudWatch alarms for constraint violations.
questions.explanation_text:
**Drift monitoring** is most useful when you match the monitoring type to the kind of change you need to detect. In this scenario, the first signal is a change in live input features after a new referral channel is introduced, while labels arrive too late to support timely quality scoring. SageMaker Model Monitor data quality monitoring is designed for this pattern: it uses a baseline of feature statistics and constraints, compares captured production inference data against that baseline, and emits monitoring results that can be surfaced through CloudWatch alarms.

Model quality monitoring is a different control loop. It evaluates whether predictions remain accurate by comparing predictions with ground truth labels, so it is valuable when labels are available but is not the best fit for unlabeled feature drift. Clarify bias drift and feature attribution drift are also important, but they answer narrower questions about fairness metrics or changes in how features influence predictions rather than the general statistical drift described here.

CloudTrail and CloudTrail Insights help with governance and audit by recording API activity and detecting unusual management event patterns. They are not model observability tools for inference payloads. For more information, see Monitor data and model quality, bias, and feature attribution drift with Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor and Monitor data quality.

questions.question_text:
A marine logistics provider's ML platform team uses AWS CodePipeline and AWS CodeBuild to package inference containers, push images to Amazon ECR, and start Amazon SageMaker Pipelines for model validation and deployment. A security review requires the team to remove plaintext credentials from the pipeline, reduce overly broad permissions, and keep build artifacts protected. The team wants to keep the existing CI/CD workflow with minimal redesign.

Which action will best meet these requirements?
questions.question_html: A marine logistics provider's ML platform team uses AWS CodePipeline and AWS CodeBuild to package inference containers, push images to Amazon ECR, and start Amazon SageMaker Pipelines for model validation and deployment. A security review requires the team to remove plaintext credentials from the pipeline, reduce overly broad permissions, and keep build artifacts protected. The team wants to keep the existing CI/CD workflow with minimal redesign. Which action will best meet these requirements?

options.A: Store secrets as plaintext CodeBuild environment variables, restrict console access to the pipeline, and rotate the variables after each release.
options.B: Store secrets in AWS Secrets Manager, encrypt pipeline artifacts with AWS KMS, and scope pipeline service roles to required actions.
options.C: Store secrets as encrypted strings in the source repository, enable CloudTrail logging, and grant AdministratorAccess to build roles.
options.D: Store secrets in an Amazon S3 artifact bucket, enable bucket versioning, and allow the pipeline role full access to the bucket.

options_list: Store secrets as plaintext CodeBuild environment variables, restrict console access to the pipeline, and rotate the variables after each release.
Store secrets in AWS Secrets Manager, encrypt pipeline artifacts with AWS KMS, and scope pipeline service roles to required actions.
Store secrets as encrypted strings in the source repository, enable CloudTrail logging, and grant AdministratorAccess to build roles.
Store secrets in an Amazon S3 artifact bucket, enable bucket versioning, and allow the pipeline role full access to the bucket.
correct_answers_text: Store secrets in AWS Secrets Manager, encrypt pipeline artifacts with AWS KMS, and scope pipeline service roles to required actions.
questions.explanation_text:
Secure ML CI/CD pipelines should treat the pipeline as a privileged production system, not just as developer tooling. Build and deployment automation often has permissions to create containers, read datasets or artifacts, update endpoints, and start SageMaker workflows, so a compromised pipeline can directly affect production models.

The best approach combines **least privilege**, **managed secret storage**, and **artifact encryption**. Sensitive values should be retrieved from a purpose-built service such as AWS Secrets Manager rather than being embedded in pipeline definitions, buildspec files, source code, or action configuration. IAM roles for CodePipeline and CodeBuild should allow only the actions needed, such as reading required artifacts, pushing to the intended ECR repository, and invoking the approved SageMaker workflow.

Encryption of pipeline artifacts with AWS KMS helps protect intermediate build outputs and deployment packages while they are stored in Amazon S3. CloudTrail and CloudWatch are still valuable for audit and monitoring, but they do not replace preventive controls such as removing plaintext secrets and narrowing permissions. See CodePipeline security best practices, Configure server-side encryption for artifacts stored in Amazon S3 for CodePipeline, Data protection in AWS CodeBuild, and Security best practices in IAM.

questions.question_text:
A regional grocery cooperative's inventory analytics team runs a product demand prediction model on an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint. The team needs to detect whether live inference requests are drifting from the feature distributions observed during training. The team also wants notifications when quality deviations occur, with the least amount of custom monitoring code.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
questions.question_html: A regional grocery cooperative's inventory analytics team runs a product demand prediction model on an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint. The team needs to detect whether live inference requests are drifting from the feature distributions observed during training. The team also wants notifications when quality deviations occur, with the least amount of custom monitoring code. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Create CloudWatch alarms for endpoint invocations, latency, and CPU utilization, and notify the team when operational thresholds change.
options.B: Enable endpoint data capture, create a baseline from training data, and schedule monitoring jobs that publish drift violations to CloudWatch.
options.C: Enable CloudTrail Insights for SageMaker API activity, and route unusual account write events to EventBridge for notification.
options.D: Track model versions in SageMaker Experiments, and compare training trial metrics before approving the next endpoint deployment.

options_list: Create CloudWatch alarms for endpoint invocations, latency, and CPU utilization, and notify the team when operational thresholds change.
Enable endpoint data capture, create a baseline from training data, and schedule monitoring jobs that publish drift violations to CloudWatch.
Enable CloudTrail Insights for SageMaker API activity, and route unusual account write events to EventBridge for notification.
Track model versions in SageMaker Experiments, and compare training trial metrics before approving the next endpoint deployment.
correct_answers_text: Enable endpoint data capture, create a baseline from training data, and schedule monitoring jobs that publish drift violations to CloudWatch.
questions.explanation_text:
**Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor** is the managed service designed for this kind of production inference monitoring. A common pattern is to enable **data capture** on a SageMaker endpoint, store captured inference inputs and outputs in Amazon S3, create a baseline from representative training or validation data, and run scheduled monitoring jobs that compare current traffic with that baseline. For more detail, see Monitor data and model quality with Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor and Capture data from deployed models.

CloudWatch remains part of the solution, but it plays a different role. **CloudWatch endpoint metrics** are appropriate for monitoring operational behavior, such as invocation rates, latency, errors, and resource utilization, while Model Monitor provides the ML-specific comparison against baselines and can publish metrics or violations for alarming. See Monitor Amazon SageMaker with Amazon CloudWatch and Monitor data quality.

CloudTrail and CloudTrail Insights are governance and audit tools for API activity in an AWS account, not tools for inspecting model inputs and outputs. SageMaker Experiments is useful during development for comparing training runs, but it does not replace runtime monitoring of deployed inference traffic.

questions.question_text:
A renewable energy trading desk's ML engineering team trained a custom PyTorch price-forecasting model. The model artifacts are stored in Amazon S3, and the inference code is available in a container image. The team needs to deploy a persistent endpoint for low-latency validation requests from a notebook before promoting the model. The team wants to define deployment settings in Python code and avoid maintaining infrastructure templates for this validation step.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
questions.question_html: A renewable energy trading desk's ML engineering team trained a custom PyTorch price-forecasting model. The model artifacts are stored in Amazon S3, and the inference code is available in a container image. The team needs to deploy a persistent endpoint for low-latency validation requests from a notebook before promoting the model. The team wants to define deployment settings in Python code and avoid maintaining infrastructure templates for this validation step. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.A: Use the SageMaker Python SDK to build the model object and call deploy to create a real-time endpoint.
options.B: Use SageMaker batch transform to process validation records and write prediction output to Amazon S3.
options.C: Use AWS CloudFormation to define SageMaker model, endpoint configuration, and endpoint resources for validation.
options.D: Use SageMaker JumpStart to select a pretrained model and deploy it to a preconfigured real-time endpoint.

options_list: Use the SageMaker Python SDK to build the model object and call deploy to create a real-time endpoint.
Use SageMaker batch transform to process validation records and write prediction output to Amazon S3.
Use AWS CloudFormation to define SageMaker model, endpoint configuration, and endpoint resources for validation.

correct_answers_text: Use the SageMaker Python SDK to build the model object and call deploy to create a real-time endpoint.
questions.explanation_text:
For a custom model that is already trained and stored as artifacts, **Amazon SageMaker AI real-time inference** is the deployment pattern for persistent, low-latency request and response validation. The SageMaker Python SDK provides a practical developer workflow from a notebook: define the model and deployment settings in code, deploy an endpoint, then use a predictor or endpoint invocation to run smoke tests.

The key tradeoff is between *developer velocity* and *deployment governance*. For notebook-based validation, the SDK avoids the extra work of writing CloudFormation resources while still creating the SageMaker model, endpoint configuration, and endpoint resources behind the scenes. CloudFormation is better suited when the team needs fully repeatable infrastructure as code for production promotion or regulated release pipelines.

**SageMaker JumpStart** is optimized for quickly deploying pretrained models from a catalog, not for substituting a team's already trained custom model. **Batch transform** is a different inference mode, it processes datasets asynchronously and stores results, rather than keeping an endpoint available for interactive validation requests.

For more information, see High-level SageMaker AI deployment options, Real-time endpoint deployment workflow, and ModelBuilder guide.

questions.question_text:
A telemedicine provider's ML team trains an Amazon SageMaker built-in XGBoost binary classification model to predict appointment no-shows. The model has high performance on the training dataset but substantially lower performance on the validation dataset. The team observes that the boosted trees are becoming overly complex and wants to make a hyperparameter change that directly limits the complexity of each tree while keeping the same algorithm and dataset.

Which action will best meet this requirement?
questions.question_html: A telemedicine provider's ML team trains an Amazon SageMaker built-in XGBoost binary classification model to predict appointment no-shows. The model has high performance on the training dataset but substantially lower performance on the validation dataset. The team observes that the boosted trees are becoming overly complex and wants to make a hyperparameter change that directly limits the complexity of each tree while keeping the same algorithm and dataset. Which action will best meet this requirement?

options.A: Increase the max_depth hyperparameter to capture more feature interactions in each boosted tree.
options.B: Increase the num_round hyperparameter to add more boosting iterations during training.
options.C: Change the eval_metric hyperparameter to report a different validation metric during training.
options.D: Reduce the max_depth hyperparameter to constrain how deep each boosted tree can grow.

options_list: Increase the max_depth hyperparameter to capture more feature interactions in each boosted tree.
Increase the num_round hyperparameter to add more boosting iterations during training.
Change the eval_metric hyperparameter to report a different validation metric during training.
Reduce the max_depth hyperparameter to constrain how deep each boosted tree can grow.
correct_answers_text: Reduce the max_depth hyperparameter to constrain how deep each boosted tree can grow.
questions.explanation_text:
In **XGBoost**, model capacity is strongly affected by tree-structure hyperparameters. The `max_depth` hyperparameter limits how deep each boosted tree can grow, so lowering it is a direct way to make each tree simpler and reduce the risk that the model memorizes training-specific patterns. This is a common response when the model performs well on training data but much worse on validation data, which is a classic sign of *overfitting*.

Other hyperparameters affect training in different ways. Increasing `num_round` usually gives the model more boosting iterations, which can increase capacity if not controlled by early stopping or other regularization. Changing `eval_metric` can change how training progress is measured, but it does not by itself reduce tree complexity. SageMaker automatic model tuning can search over hyperparameter ranges and select the best training job based on an objective metric, but the engineer still needs to understand which hyperparameters affect model complexity. For more information, see SageMaker XGBoost hyperparameters and SageMaker AI Automatic Model Tuning overview.

questions.question_text:
A digital advertising analytics team runs a nightly Spark feature-engineering workload on Amazon EMR before training a recommendation model. The cluster reads raw logs from Amazon S3 and writes curated features back to S3. The team uses HDFS only for intermediate processing data and must reduce compute cost while avoiding unnecessary risk to the cluster's storage and coordination roles.

Which purchasing strategy should the team use for the EMR cluster?
questions.question_html: A digital advertising analytics team runs a nightly Spark feature-engineering workload on Amazon EMR before training a recommendation model. The cluster reads raw logs from Amazon S3 and writes curated features back to S3. The team uses HDFS only for intermediate processing data and must reduce compute cost while avoiding unnecessary risk to the cluster's storage and coordination roles. Which purchasing strategy should the team use for the EMR cluster?

options.A: Run the entire EMR cluster on On-Demand Instances, and rely on AWS Budgets alerts for cost control.
options.B: Purchase Reserved Instances for the task node fleet, and keep master and core nodes on On-Demand Instances.
options.C: Run the master and core node groups on On-Demand Instances, and add Spot Instances only as task nodes.
options.D: Run the master, core, and task node groups on Spot Instances, and increase HDFS replication settings.

options_list: Run the entire EMR cluster on On-Demand Instances, and rely on AWS Budgets alerts for cost control.
Purchase Reserved Instances for the task node fleet, and keep master and core nodes on On-Demand Instances.
Run the master and core node groups on On-Demand Instances, and add Spot Instances only as task nodes.
Run the master, core, and task node groups on Spot Instances, and increase HDFS replication settings.
correct_answers_text: Run the master and core node groups on On-Demand Instances, and add Spot Instances only as task nodes.
questions.explanation_text:
For Amazon EMR clusters, the **node role** matters when selecting a purchasing option. Master nodes coordinate the cluster, core nodes run tasks and store data in HDFS, and task nodes run tasks without storing HDFS data. Because task nodes are optional compute capacity, they are a good place to use lower-cost **Spot Instances** when the workload can tolerate task interruption or retry.

Using Spot Instances for master or core nodes is a common cost anti-pattern unless the workload is experimental or the team is extremely cost sensitive. If a core node that stores HDFS blocks is interrupted, the cluster can be exposed to partial data loss or job disruption. Keeping master and core nodes on **On-Demand Instances** preserves stability while still reducing cost by adding Spot capacity for task nodes.

**AWS Budgets** is useful for alerts and governance, but it does not itself choose cheaper capacity. Reserved Instances and Savings Plans are better aligned with sustained, predictable usage commitments, while Spot Instances are designed for spare capacity that can be interrupted. For purchasing option comparisons, see Amazon EC2 instance purchasing options and Amazon EC2 Spot Instances.

The team is preparing a real-time inference endpoint and is unsure whether CPU instances will meet the latency target or whether GPU instances are needed. The team wants to compare candidate endpoint configurations under expected traffic before choosing production compute resources.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST custom testing effort?

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST custom testing effort?

options.A: Enable SageMaker Training Compiler on a GPU training job and use the compiled training result to choose the endpoint instance type.
options.B: Create SageMaker Processing jobs on candidate CPU and GPU instances and compare CloudWatch utilization metrics from each processing job.
options.C: Register the model in SageMaker Model Registry and run a SageMaker Inference Recommender endpoint recommendation job with candidate CPU and GPU instances.
options.D: Deploy the model to two SageMaker production variants and split live traffic evenly across candidate CPU and GPU instances.

questions.explanation_text:
**SageMaker Inference Recommender** is designed for the decision point in this scenario: selecting an inference instance type and endpoint configuration based on measured behavior instead of guesswork. The course material describes two modes: instance recommendations, which run load tests on recommended instance types, and endpoint recommendations, which use a custom load test where you specify candidate instances, traffic patterns, latency requirements, and throughput requirements.

For production hosting, SageMaker defines compute resources through endpoint configurations and production variants. A production variant includes resources such as the hosting instance type and initial instance count, and it can also be used for traffic splitting once a deployment strategy has been chosen. The relevant documentation describes endpoint configurations in CreateEndpointConfig and production variant resource settings in ProductionVariant.

Splitting live traffic between variants can be useful for A/B testing, but it is not the least-risk way to answer an initial CPU versus GPU sizing question. Processing jobs and training optimizations also solve different problems: processing jobs run data processing or evaluation code, and Training Compiler optimizes certain training workloads. For inference capacity planning, the better mental model is to benchmark the *serving path*, including model container startup, request handling, latency, throughput, and cost per inference, before selecting the endpoint compute.

For more context, see the SageMaker guidance on Test models in production and the training compute overview in Train a Model with Amazon SageMaker.

A museum consortium's digital archives team stores visitor survey exports in Amazon S3. The exports include names, email addresses, and free-form comments. Data stewards need a visual workflow to profile the data, apply repeatable transformations that mask or delete personally identifiable information, and run the transformations as a managed job that writes cleaned datasets back to Amazon S3. The team wants to avoid writing Spark code or maintaining processing clusters.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.D: Use AWS Glue DataBrew to profile the dataset, build a transformation recipe, and run a recipe job that writes output to Amazon S3.

It is a strong choice for general ETL pipelines, especially when engineers need DAG-style workflows, joins, and transforms across sources, but it is not the lowest-overhead choice for non-coding stewards who need profiling and reusable PII cleansing recipes. **Amazon EMR with Spark** is powerful for large-scale transformations, but it introduces code and cluster lifecycle concerns that the scenario explicitly wants to avoid.

questions.question_text:
A biomedical device manufacturer's ML team trains a PyTorch convolutional model on tens of millions of labeled sensor images by using Amazon SageMaker. The model fits in GPU memory on a single instance, but each training run takes too long because the dataset is large. The team wants to reduce wall clock training time by using multiple GPU instances while preserving the model architecture.

Which solution is most appropriate?
questions.question_html: A biomedical device manufacturer's ML team trains a PyTorch convolutional model on tens of millions of labeled sensor images by using Amazon SageMaker. The model fits in GPU memory on a single instance, but each training run takes too long because the dataset is large. The team wants to reduce wall clock training time by using multiple GPU instances while preserving the model architecture. Which solution is most appropriate?

options.A: Increase the number of parallel automatic model tuning jobs, use random search, and compare more hyperparameter combinations at once.
options.B: Enable SageMaker Training Compiler, keep the existing distributed training configuration, and compile the model on GPU instances.
options.C: Enable SageMaker Distributed Data Parallel, initialize PyTorch with the smddp backend, and run the training job across multiple GPU instances.
options.D: Enable SageMaker model parallelism, shard the model layers across GPUs, and keep the same dataset on each training instance.

options_list: Increase the number of parallel automatic model tuning jobs, use random search, and compare more hyperparameter combinations at once.
Enable SageMaker Training Compiler, keep the existing distributed training configuration, and compile the model on GPU instances.
Enable SageMaker Distributed Data Parallel, initialize PyTorch with the smddp backend, and run the training job across multiple GPU instances.
Enable SageMaker model parallelism, shard the model layers across GPUs, and keep the same dataset on each training instance.
correct_answers_text: Enable SageMaker Distributed Data Parallel, initialize PyTorch with the smddp backend, and run the training job across multiple GPU instances.
questions.explanation_text:
When a training job is slow because the **dataset is large** and the model already fits on a single GPU, the usual distributed training pattern is **data parallelism**. Each worker processes a different slice of each batch, computes gradients, and synchronizes updates so the model learns as if it were training on the combined data. SageMaker provides distributed training libraries for this pattern, including PyTorch integration that can use the `smddp` backend, as described in SageMaker distributed training and Get started with distributed training.

**Model parallelism** solves a different problem: the model itself is too large for one device, or the team wants to partition model state and activations across GPUs. That adds communication and implementation overhead, so it is not the best first choice when the architecture already fits in memory. **Training Compiler** and **automatic model tuning** can reduce training cost or improve model quality in other situations, but they do not directly match the stated need to distribute one PyTorch training run across multiple GPU instances. For early stopping in tuning jobs, see Use early stopping.

questions.section: Content Domain 1: Data Preparation for Machine Learning (ML)
questions.question_text:
A public library network's digital services team is preparing training data for three supervised ML models: a tabular model that predicts overdue account risk, a text classifier that routes patron support messages, and an image classifier that identifies damaged returned materials. Data profiling shows class imbalance in each dataset, with valid minority-class examples that are much rarer than majority-class examples. The team cannot collect enough new real-world examples before the next training cycle and wants to preserve as much existing data as possible.

Which TWO actions should the team take to address the imbalance before training?
questions.question_html: A public library network's digital services team is preparing training data for three supervised ML models: a tabular model that predicts overdue account risk, a text classifier that routes patron support messages, and an image classifier that identifies damaged returned materials. Data profiling shows class imbalance in each dataset, with valid minority-class examples that are much rarer than majority-class examples. The team cannot collect enough new real-world examples before the next training cycle and wants to preserve as much existing data as possible. Which TWO actions should the team take to address the imbalance before training?

options.A: Apply random oversampling to the majority classes to preserve the original class distribution.
options.B: Apply random undersampling to remove minority-class examples from each training dataset.
options.C: Generate label-preserving augmented examples for minority-class text and image records before training.
options.D: Apply random oversampling or SMOTE to increase minority-class representation in the tabular dataset.
options.E: Run a SageMaker Clarify CI report after training and keep the training data unchanged.

options_list: Apply random oversampling to the majority classes to preserve the original class distribution.
Apply random undersampling to remove minority-class examples from each training dataset.
Generate label-preserving augmented examples for minority-class text and image records before training.
Apply random oversampling or SMOTE to increase minority-class representation in the tabular dataset.
Run a SageMaker Clarify CI report after training and keep the training data unchanged.
correct_answers_text: Generate label-preserving augmented examples for minority-class text and image records before training.
Apply random oversampling or SMOTE to increase minority-class representation in the tabular dataset.
questions.explanation_text:
**Class Imbalance (CI)** means that one class or facet has fewer examples than another. In supervised learning, this often causes the model to learn majority-class patterns well while performing poorly on the minority class, even when overall accuracy looks acceptable. SageMaker Clarify includes a CI metric for identifying this kind of imbalance before training, as described in Class Imbalance and the broader pre-training bias metrics documentation.

When the team wants to preserve existing data, **oversampling** and **synthetic data generation** are usually better fits than removing data. For tabular numeric data, random oversampling duplicates minority examples, while SMOTE creates synthetic minority examples from neighboring samples. SageMaker Data Wrangler documents balance-data approaches such as random oversampling, random undersampling, and SMOTE in Transform data.

For image and text datasets, **label-preserving augmentation** can increase minority-class coverage when new labeled data is hard to obtain. Image augmentation might create transformed versions that retain the same label, while text augmentation must be handled carefully so that meaning and label are preserved. For image workloads, SageMaker image classification documentation includes augmentation-related options in Image Classification hyperparameters.

Undersampling can be useful only when it removes majority-class examples in a controlled way, and it trades lower imbalance for less training data. Removing minority examples, oversampling majority examples, or only measuring CI without changing the dataset fails to address the root problem.

questions.explanation_text:
Reproducible ML development requires more than saving a final model file. Engineers need to preserve the **context** that produced the model: input data, transformations, training parameters, metrics, code path, and resulting artifacts. **SageMaker Experiments** addresses the comparison side of this problem by helping teams organize trials and evaluate how different feature transformations, algorithms, or hyperparameters affected results. For related managed experiment tracking capabilities, see Track experiments with MLflow.

**SageMaker Pipelines** addresses the workflow side by turning the training and evaluation process into a repeatable managed workflow instead of a sequence of ad hoc notebook cells. Combining pipelines with **Model Registry** and **ML Lineage Tracking** gives the team a stronger audit trail for model versions and the datasets, jobs, parameters, and artifacts connected to them. CloudWatch Logs Insights and QuickSight are useful supporting tools for operational log analysis and visualization, but they do not replace experiment tracking, workflow orchestration, or lineage. Date-stamped folders are a common anti-pattern because they rely on manual discipline rather than managed metadata and reproducible execution. See Amazon SageMaker Pipelines, Amazon SageMaker ML Lineage Tracking, and Register and deploy models with Model Registry.

Reproducible ML development requires more than saving a final model file. Engineers need to preserve the context that produced the model: input data, transformations, training parameters, metrics, code path, and resulting artifacts. SageMaker Experiments addresses the comparison side of this problem by helping teams organize trials and evaluate how different feature transformations, algorithms, or hyperparameters affected results. For related managed experiment tracking capabilities, see Track experiments with MLflow.

SageMaker Pipelines addresses the workflow side by turning the training and evaluation process into a repeatable managed workflow instead of a sequence of ad hoc notebook cells. Combining pipelines with Model Registry and ML Lineage Tracking gives the team a stronger audit trail for model versions and the datasets, jobs, parameters, and artifacts connected to them. CloudWatch Logs Insights and QuickSight are useful supporting tools for operational log analysis and visualization, but they do not replace experiment tracking, workflow orchestration, or lineage. Date-stamped folders are a common anti-pattern because they rely on manual discipline rather than managed metadata and reproducible execution. See Amazon SageMaker Pipelines, Amazon SageMaker ML Lineage Tracking, and Register and deploy models with Model Registry.

A professional sports league's fan engagement analytics team receives continuous JSON clickstream events from mobile apps and venue kiosks. The team needs to store the events in an Amazon S3 data lake for later ML feature exploration with SQL-based tools. The team does not need to replay records after delivery. The team wants the lowest operational overhead for ingestion, buffering, basic transformation, and schema discovery.

Which TWO steps will meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Deploy Amazon Kinesis Data Streams and build consumers to write events to Amazon S3.
options.B: Create an Amazon MSK cluster and write Kafka consumers to persist events to Amazon S3.
options.C: Configure Amazon Data Firehose to deliver the event stream to Amazon S3.
options.D: Run an AWS Glue crawler on the Amazon S3 data lake prefixes.
options.E: Use Amazon Athena as the primary service to ingest and transform streaming events.

options_list: Deploy Amazon Kinesis Data Streams and build consumers to write events to Amazon S3.
Create an Amazon MSK cluster and write Kafka consumers to persist events to Amazon S3.
Configure Amazon Data Firehose to deliver the event stream to Amazon S3.
Run an AWS Glue crawler on the Amazon S3 data lake prefixes.

questions.explanation_text:
**Amazon Data Firehose** is designed for managed streaming ingestion into storage and analytics destinations. It reduces operational work because it handles delivery, buffering, scaling, and optional record transformation before data lands in Amazon S3. This fits a data lake ingestion pattern when the team wants near real-time delivery but does not require the replay model of a stream processing platform. See Amazon Data Firehose overview.

After the data is stored in **Amazon S3**, the team still needs metadata so SQL-based tools can understand the data layout. An **AWS Glue crawler** can inspect S3 locations, infer schemas, and populate the AWS Glue Data Catalog, which services such as Athena can use for querying. See AWS Glue crawlers and Amazon S3 fundamentals.

Kinesis Data Streams and Amazon MSK are plausible streaming choices, but they are better suited when the workload needs custom stream processing, consumer applications, Kafka compatibility, or replay behavior. Those capabilities are valuable tradeoffs, but they add engineering work that is not justified by this scenario. Athena is also commonly used with S3 data lakes, but it is a query engine rather than the component that continuously ingests event streams.

questions.section: Content Domain 4: ML Solution Monitoring, Maintenance, and S
questions.question_text:
A maritime logistics carrier's ML platform team trains Amazon SageMaker models on sensitive customs document features stored in Amazon S3. The security team requires the training environment to run without direct internet access and to access only an approved S3 bucket for training data and model artifacts. The solution must use network isolation controls in the VPC while allowing the training job to complete.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
questions.question_html: A maritime logistics carrier's ML platform team trains Amazon SageMaker models on sensitive customs document features stored in Amazon S3. The security team requires the training environment to run without direct internet access and to access only an approved S3 bucket for training data and model artifacts. The solution must use network isolation controls in the VPC while allowing the training job to complete. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Configure the training job with network isolation enabled and no VPC endpoints. Add an IAM role that allows access to the approved bucket.
options.B: Configure the training job with private VPC subnets and a NAT gateway route. Add unrestricted outbound rules and CloudTrail auditing for the bucket.
options.C: Configure the training job with private VPC subnets and restrictive security groups. Add an Amazon S3 VPC endpoint with endpoint and bucket policies for the approved bucket.
options.D: Configure the training job with public VPC subnets and restrictive security groups. Add an internet gateway route and bucket policies for the approved bucket.

options_list: Configure the training job with network isolation enabled and no VPC endpoints. Add an IAM role that allows access to the approved bucket.
Configure the training job with private VPC subnets and a NAT gateway route. Add unrestricted outbound rules and CloudTrail auditing for the bucket.
Configure the training job with private VPC subnets and restrictive security groups. Add an Amazon S3 VPC endpoint with endpoint and bucket policies for the approved bucket.
Configure the training job with public VPC subnets and restrictive security groups. Add an internet gateway route and bucket policies for the approved bucket.
correct_answers_text: Configure the training job with private VPC subnets and restrictive security groups. Add an Amazon S3 VPC endpoint with endpoint and bucket policies for the approved bucket.
questions.explanation_text:
For a secure SageMaker training setup, think of the VPC as the network boundary, the subnet as the placement choice, and the security group as the workload-level firewall. SageMaker training jobs can be configured with specific VPC subnets and security groups so the training containers are attached to the intended private network rather than using a default internet-enabled path. The SageMaker documentation describes this pattern in Give SageMaker Training Jobs Access to Resources in Your Amazon VPC and Give SageMaker Jobs Access to Resources in Your Amazon VPC.

Because the training data and artifacts are in Amazon S3, the private subnet design still needs a private route to S3 when the requirement is to use VPC network controls for S3 access. An **Amazon S3 VPC endpoint** provides that path without requiring the training environment to reach S3 through the public internet, and policies on the endpoint and bucket help narrow access to the approved bucket. Security groups should be scoped to the traffic the training containers actually need, following the same least-privilege mindset described for security groups in Control Traffic to Resources Using Security Groups.

Using public subnets or a NAT gateway can be valid in other architectures, but those choices conflict with a requirement for no direct internet access. SageMaker network isolation is useful when you need to prevent the training container from making outbound network calls, but by itself it is not the same as placing the job in private VPC subnets with security groups and endpoint policy controls. Subnet placement and subnet-level controls are foundational VPC design decisions, as summarized in Amazon VPC Basics and Configure Subnets.

questions.section: Content Domain 2: ML Model Development
questions.question_text:
An energy retailer's demand forecasting team trains a PyTorch neural network in Amazon SageMaker. The training script emits the validation RMSE after each epoch. The team runs automatic model tuning every week, but random search is consuming too many training hours without consistent gains. The team can tolerate some parallel training, but wants to reduce wasted trials and avoid tuning unimportant hyperparameters while preserving model quality.

Which approach best meets these requirements?
questions.question_html: An energy retailer's demand forecasting team trains a PyTorch neural network in Amazon SageMaker. The training script emits the validation RMSE after each epoch. The team runs automatic model tuning every week, but random search is consuming too many training hours without consistent gains. The team can tolerate some parallel training, but wants to reduce wasted trials and avoid tuning unimportant hyperparameters while preserving model quality. Which approach best meets these requirements?

options.A: Configure SageMaker automatic model tuning to use grid search, and include every available hyperparameter in the search space.
options.B: Configure SageMaker automatic model tuning to use Hyperband with early stopping, and tune only the highest-impact hyperparameters.
options.C: Replace the single training job with SageMaker distributed data parallel training, and keep manual tuning outside automatic model tuning.
options.D: Increase the maximum number of parallel random-search training jobs, and keep the current hyperparameter search space.

options_list: Configure SageMaker automatic model tuning to use grid search, and include every available hyperparameter in the search space.
Configure SageMaker automatic model tuning to use Hyperband with early stopping, and tune only the highest-impact hyperparameters.
Replace the single training job with SageMaker distributed data parallel training, and keep manual tuning outside automatic model tuning.
Increase the maximum number of parallel random-search training jobs, and keep the current hyperparameter search space.
correct_answers_text: Configure SageMaker automatic model tuning to use Hyperband with early stopping, and tune only the highest-impact hyperparameters.
questions.explanation_text:
**Hyperparameter tuning** is a tradeoff between exploring enough configurations to improve the objective metric and avoiding training jobs that are unlikely to pay off. For iterative training workloads, such as neural networks that report a validation metric after each epoch, **Hyperband** can use early results to stop poor trials and focus resources on more promising configurations. This is why it is a better fit than simply adding more parallel random trials when the goal is to improve both training efficiency and model quality.

Search space design matters as much as the tuning algorithm. Tuning every possible hyperparameter can cause the number of combinations to grow quickly, which increases cost and can make it harder to find useful improvements. A practical ML engineer should focus automatic tuning on the hyperparameters that are most likely to affect the objective metric, then use completion limits or early stopping behavior to control resource usage.

Grid search is usually the least efficient choice in this scenario because it is brute force and does not learn from previous trials. Random search is more parallelizable, but it still wastes work when the search space is too broad. Distributed training addresses the speed of individual training jobs, not the quality or efficiency of hyperparameter selection, and it can add overhead that is not justified if the main bottleneck is poor trial selection.

For more information, see Overview of SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning and How SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning works.

questions.question_text:
A regional airline's predictive maintenance team receives daily CSV files in Amazon S3 from aircraft maintenance systems. Before the files are used for feature engineering, the team must validate recurring checks such as missing values, unexpected values, and duplicate records. Data analysts need a visual, managed workflow with minimal custom code and repeatable validation results for each dataset refresh.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
questions.question_html: A regional airline's predictive maintenance team receives daily CSV files in Amazon S3 from aircraft maintenance systems. Before the files are used for feature engineering, the team must validate recurring checks such as missing values, unexpected values, and duplicate records. Data analysts need a visual, managed workflow with minimal custom code and repeatable validation results for each dataset refresh. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.A: Create a SageMaker Model Monitor schedule, build a production baseline, and review drift alerts after deployment.
options.B: Create an AWS Glue DataBrew project, define a data quality ruleset, and run DataBrew profile jobs for each refresh.
options.C: Create an Amazon QuickSight analysis, add anomaly visuals, and review dashboards after each refresh.
options.D: Create an Amazon Macie discovery job, inspect sensitive data findings, and approve files with no alerts.

options_list: Create a SageMaker Model Monitor schedule, build a production baseline, and review drift alerts after deployment.
Create an AWS Glue DataBrew project, define a data quality ruleset, and run DataBrew profile jobs for each refresh.
Create an Amazon QuickSight analysis, add anomaly visuals, and review dashboards after each refresh.
Create an Amazon Macie discovery job, inspect sensitive data findings, and approve files with no alerts.
correct_answers_text: Create an AWS Glue DataBrew project, define a data quality ruleset, and run DataBrew profile jobs for each refresh.
questions.explanation_text:
**AWS Glue DataBrew** is designed for visual data preparation and profiling, which makes it a strong fit when analysts need to inspect and validate datasets without writing custom ETL code. A DataBrew ruleset can be associated with a dataset and evaluated as part of a profile job, so the team can repeat the same validation checks each time new files arrive.

The important mental model is that *data quality validation happens before training*. Validating missing values, unexpected values, duplicates, and similar issues helps prevent poor feature engineering decisions and reduces the chance that a model learns from corrupted or misleading data.

QuickSight can help users explore and visualize data, but using dashboards as a quality gate is an anti-pattern when the requirement is repeatable validation. Macie focuses on sensitive data discovery rather than general dataset correctness. SageMaker Model Monitor is valuable after deployment, but it monitors live model inputs and outputs relative to baselines rather than profiling raw training files before they enter the ML pipeline.

For more information, see AWS Glue DataBrew data quality validation and Creating a data quality ruleset in AWS Glue DataBrew.
