questions.section: Content Domain 1: Data Preparation for Machine Learning (ML)
questions.question_text:
A university neuroscience lab is preparing a large collection of experiment files for ML training. The files already reside on an Amazon EFS file system that is mounted by several preprocessing applications. The lab wants Amazon SageMaker training jobs to read the same files without first copying the dataset to Amazon S3. The training jobs can run inside the lab's VPC.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST data movement?
questions.question_html: A university neuroscience lab is preparing a large collection of experiment files for ML training. The files already reside on an Amazon EFS file system that is mounted by several preprocessing applications. The lab wants Amazon SageMaker training jobs to read the same files without first copying the dataset to Amazon S3. The training jobs can run inside the lab's VPC. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST data movement?

options.A: Configure S3 Fast File mode for the training job and reference the Amazon EFS mount path.
options.B: Configure the SageMaker training job to use the Amazon EFS file system as the training data source.
options.C: Copy the dataset to Amazon S3 and configure the SageMaker training job to use S3 File mode.
options.D: Migrate the dataset to Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP and mount it from the SageMaker training job.

options_list: Configure S3 Fast File mode for the training job and reference the Amazon EFS mount path.
Configure the SageMaker training job to use the Amazon EFS file system as the training data source.
Copy the dataset to Amazon S3 and configure the SageMaker training job to use S3 File mode.
Migrate the dataset to Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP and mount it from the SageMaker training job.
correct_answers_text: Configure the SageMaker training job to use the Amazon EFS file system as the training data source.
questions.explanation_text:
**Amazon EFS** is a shared, elastic file system that can be mounted by multiple clients in a VPC, which makes it a good fit when preprocessing applications and training jobs need to work from the same file tree. In SageMaker training, EFS is appropriate when the dataset is already in EFS and the training job is configured to run with VPC access. This avoids a separate data-copy step to Amazon S3, which is useful when the requirement is minimizing data movement rather than optimizing for an S3-native training workflow.

**Amazon S3** remains the most common storage source for SageMaker training and supports input modes such as File mode, Fast File mode, and Pipe mode. However, those modes are S3-oriented and do not turn an EFS path into an S3 source. **Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP** is a strong choice when an organization needs managed ONTAP capabilities, multiprotocol access, or migration of existing NetApp/NAS workflows, but introducing it here would move data away from the storage service that already satisfies the requirement. For more details, see Access Training Data in SageMaker AI, What is Amazon Elastic File System?, and What is Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP?.

questions.section: Content Domain 1: Data Preparation for Machine Learning (ML)
questions.question_text:
A subscription fitness app's ML team stores monthly CSV exports in Amazon S3 for churn model training. The exports contain email addresses and phone numbers that are needed only to join records across months. Analysts must not access the plaintext values, and the prepared output must keep the same transformed value for the same original value so joins still work. The team wants a repeatable visual data preparation approach with minimal custom code.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
questions.question_html: A subscription fitness app's ML team stores monthly CSV exports in Amazon S3 for churn model training. The exports contain email addresses and phone numbers that are needed only to join records across months. Analysts must not access the plaintext values, and the prepared output must keep the same transformed value for the same original value so joins still work. The team wants a repeatable visual data preparation approach with minimal custom code. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Configure Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery on the S3 bucket, then review findings before granting analysts access.
options.B: Apply AWS Lake Formation LF-Tags to classify the tables, then grant analysts tag-based access to the restricted columns.
options.C: Run an AWS Glue DataBrew profile job with PII statistics, then apply probabilistic encryption in a recipe to the PII columns.
options.D: Run an AWS Glue DataBrew profile job with PII statistics, then apply deterministic encryption in a recipe to the PII columns.

options_list: Configure Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery on the S3 bucket, then review findings before granting analysts access.
Apply AWS Lake Formation LF-Tags to classify the tables, then grant analysts tag-based access to the restricted columns.
Run an AWS Glue DataBrew profile job with PII statistics, then apply probabilistic encryption in a recipe to the PII columns.
Run an AWS Glue DataBrew profile job with PII statistics, then apply deterministic encryption in a recipe to the PII columns.
correct_answers_text: Run an AWS Glue DataBrew profile job with PII statistics, then apply deterministic encryption in a recipe to the PII columns.
questions.explanation_text:
**AWS Glue DataBrew** is designed for visual, repeatable data preparation, including PII identification and protection steps. In this scenario, the important nuance is not only hiding email addresses and phone numbers, but also keeping a stable replacement value so records from different months can still be joined. A DataBrew profile job can help identify PII, and a recipe can apply transformations such as masking, hashing, or encryption before writing prepared data back to Amazon S3.

**Deterministic encryption** is the best match when equality must be preserved after obfuscation, because the same original value can be transformed consistently. Probabilistic encryption is useful when stronger non-repeatability is desired, but that property works against the join requirement. Amazon Macie helps classify and alert on sensitive data in S3, but it is not the transformation step that produces a sanitized ML-ready dataset. Lake Formation LF-Tags are useful for governance and access control, but tagging or restricting access is different from anonymizing values for model development.

For more information, see AWS Glue DataBrew personal information protection, Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery, and AWS Lake Formation tag-based access control.

questions.question_text:
An online grocery retailer's personalization team hosts a recommendation model on an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint. The team has trained a replacement model and wants to compare the replacement model against the current model by using live request patterns. The replacement model must not return responses to customers until the team confirms that its prediction behavior and latency are acceptable.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
questions.question_html: An online grocery retailer's personalization team hosts a recommendation model on an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint. The team has trained a replacement model and wants to compare the replacement model against the current model by using live request patterns. The replacement model must not return responses to customers until the team confirms that its prediction behavior and latency are acceptable. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Deploy the replacement model to a separate SageMaker endpoint and replay a stored validation dataset to both endpoints.
options.B: Replace the current model during an off-peak window and use SageMaker Model Monitor to detect quality changes.
options.C: Create a SageMaker shadow test with the current model as the production variant and the replacement model as the shadow variant.
options.D: Add the replacement model as a SageMaker production variant with a small traffic weight and increase the weight after review.

options_list: Deploy the replacement model to a separate SageMaker endpoint and replay a stored validation dataset to both endpoints.
Replace the current model during an off-peak window and use SageMaker Model Monitor to detect quality changes.
Create a SageMaker shadow test with the current model as the production variant and the replacement model as the shadow variant.
Add the replacement model as a SageMaker production variant with a small traffic weight and increase the weight after review.
correct_answers_text: Create a SageMaker shadow test with the current model as the production variant and the replacement model as the shadow variant.
questions.explanation_text:
**SageMaker shadow testing** is designed for validating a new model against the model that is already serving production traffic. The production variant continues to handle customer responses, while the shadow variant receives copied inference requests so the team can compare behavior and infrastructure performance without changing the customer-facing result. See the AWS documentation for Overview of SageMaker AI shadow tests and Creation workflow for shadow tests.

This differs from a weighted production variant rollout, where the new model actively serves some portion of live traffic. Weighted variants are appropriate when the team is ready for limited exposure, but the scenario requires observation before any customer response comes from the new model. Shadow tests also provide a practical comparison point for latency, errors, and resource behavior, which can be reviewed in SageMaker and CloudWatch as described in Monitoring shadow tests and SageMaker endpoint CloudWatch metric definitions and dimensions.

A legal research publisher's knowledge products team wants to build a prototype that generates concise summaries of long legal memos. The team wants to compare several AWS and third-party pretrained generative models through a managed API, avoid provisioning model hosting infrastructure, and pay based on usage during an unpredictable pilot.

Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.D: Use SageMaker JumpStart to deploy a selected text generation model to a SageMaker endpoint and invoke the endpoint.

questions.explanation_text:
**Amazon Bedrock** is the best fit when a team wants managed access to foundation models from AWS and third-party providers without building, training, or hosting the model infrastructure itself. Bedrock exposes model catalog and runtime capabilities so applications can call selected models through supported inference APIs, which aligns well with a pilot that needs fast comparison of generative models and variable usage. In current commercial Regions, access depends on the required account permissions, including AWS Marketplace permissions where applicable, and some providers can have additional first-use requirements. See the Amazon Bedrock documentation on Using models and Model support by feature and Region.

**SageMaker JumpStart** is also relevant to this skill because it helps users find pretrained models, foundation models, and example notebooks from SageMaker. It is a strong choice when the team wants to start from a model and then manage SageMaker training, fine-tuning, or deployment resources. For the stated requirement, however, a managed model API has less operational overhead than deploying and operating a SageMaker endpoint. The SageMaker documentation describes these capabilities in SageMaker JumpStart.

JumpStart solution templates are documented for **Studio Classic**, which is no longer available for new onboarding, so they are not the most direct choice for a new prototype that only needs managed generative model invocation. Even where templates are available, they are intended to create example resources and workflows for common ML use cases, which adds customization and lifecycle management compared with calling a foundation model API. For documented JumpStart solution template use cases, see SageMaker JumpStart solutions.

The built-in SageMaker algorithm catalog is important for choosing algorithms by ML problem type, but model selection must match the task. Algorithms such as XGBoost and Linear Learner are excellent for many structured-data problems, while legal memo summarization is a generative text task that is better served by a pretrained generative model. questions.section: Content Domain 2: ML Model Development
questions.question_text:
A biotechnology lab trains a PyTorch neural network in Amazon SageMaker to predict molecular activity. The training script publishes validation loss after each epoch. The team currently runs many manual trials across a large hyperparameter space, and many poor trials run to completion. The team wants to improve validation loss while using compute resources more efficiently.

Which solution will best meet these requirements?
questions.question_html: A biotechnology lab trains a PyTorch neural network in Amazon SageMaker to predict molecular activity. The training script publishes validation loss after each epoch. The team currently runs many manual trials across a large hyperparameter space, and many poor trials run to completion. The team wants to improve validation loss while using compute resources more efficiently. Which solution will best meet these requirements?

options.A: Use SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning with Hyperband, set validation loss as the objective metric, and tune the highest impact hyperparameters.
options.B: Use SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning with random search, set validation loss as the objective metric, and maximize parallel training jobs.
options.C: Use SageMaker Debugger with custom rules, collect epoch tensors during training, and keep the current hyperparameter search.
options.D: Use SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning with grid search, set validation loss as the objective metric, and enumerate all supported hyperparameters.

options_list: Use SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning with Hyperband, set validation loss as the objective metric, and tune the highest impact hyperparameters.
Use SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning with random search, set validation loss as the objective metric, and maximize parallel training jobs.
Use SageMaker Debugger with custom rules, collect epoch tensors during training, and keep the current hyperparameter search.
Use SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning with grid search, set validation loss as the objective metric, and enumerate all supported hyperparameters.
correct_answers_text: Use SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning with Hyperband, set validation loss as the objective metric, and tune the highest impact hyperparameters.
questions.explanation_text:
**SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning** improves model development by running multiple training jobs with different hyperparameter values and selecting the model that performs best against a chosen objective metric. In this scenario, validation loss is already emitted after each epoch, which makes the workload suitable for strategies that use intermediate training results.

**Hyperband** is designed for iterative algorithms, such as many neural network training jobs, because it can use early performance signals to allocate resources more effectively. This is a better fit than brute force grid search or broad random search when the goal is to improve model quality without wasting compute on trials that are unlikely to succeed. AWS also recommends narrowing tuning to the most important hyperparameters because large search spaces make optimization harder and more expensive.

For more information, see Perform automatic model tuning with SageMaker, How hyperparameter tuning works, Best practices for hyperparameter tuning, and Stop training jobs early.

questions.section: Content Domain 4: ML Solution Monitoring, Maintenance, and S
questions.question_text:
A digital advertising agency's ML governance team uses Amazon SageMaker AI for model training. Data scientists need to start training jobs from SageMaker Studio by using an already approved execution role. That role should read input data from one Amazon S3 prefix and write artifacts to one S3 output prefix. The team must enforce least privilege and prevent users from selecting unapproved roles for jobs.

Which actions should the team take? (Select TWO.)
questions.question_html: A digital advertising agency's ML governance team uses Amazon SageMaker AI for model training. Data scientists need to start training jobs from SageMaker Studio by using an already approved execution role. That role should read input data from one Amazon S3 prefix and write artifacts to one S3 output prefix. The team must enforce least privilege and prevent users from selecting unapproved roles for jobs. Which actions should the team take? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Grant S3 bucket access to each data scientist identity and remove data access permissions from the SageMaker execution role.
options.B: Configure the approved SageMaker execution role with SageMaker trust and least-privilege access to the required S3 prefixes and KMS key.
options.C: Grant data scientists an IAM identity policy for required SageMaker training actions and iam:PassRole on only the approved execution role.
options.D: Grant broad KMS key administrator access to the data scientists and rely on the key policy to constrain SageMaker job creation.
options.E: Attach AmazonSageMakerFullAccess and AmazonS3FullAccess to each data scientist, then review CloudTrail for misuse after jobs run.

options_list: Grant S3 bucket access to each data scientist identity and remove data access permissions from the SageMaker execution role.
Configure the approved SageMaker execution role with SageMaker trust and least-privilege access to the required S3 prefixes and KMS key.
Grant data scientists an IAM identity policy for required SageMaker training actions and iam:PassRole on only the approved execution role.
Grant broad KMS key administrator access to the data scientists and rely on the key policy to constrain SageMaker job creation.
Attach AmazonSageMakerFullAccess and AmazonS3FullAccess to each data scientist, then review CloudTrail for misuse after jobs run.
correct_answers_text: Configure the approved SageMaker execution role with SageMaker trust and least-privilege access to the required S3 prefixes and KMS key.
Grant data scientists an IAM identity policy for required SageMaker training actions and iam:PassRole on only the approved execution role.
questions.explanation_text:
For SageMaker AI training, separate the permissions of the **human or application identity** from the permissions of the **SageMaker execution role**. The user or application needs permission to call the required SageMaker APIs, and also needs `iam:PassRole` for the specific role that SageMaker is allowed to assume. Restricting `iam:PassRole` to an approved role is the control that prevents users from selecting a different role with broader access.

The execution role is the role that SageMaker assumes while running the job, so it needs a trust relationship for SageMaker and only the permissions required by the workload, such as access to the specific S3 prefixes and applicable KMS key. Attaching broad policies such as full SageMaker and full S3 access is a common anti-pattern because it makes experimentation easy but leaves production access too permissive. CloudTrail can help audit what happened, but it is not a substitute for preventive IAM controls. See the SageMaker IAM overview in Identity and Access Management for Amazon SageMaker AI, execution role guidance in SageMaker AI Roles, and `iam:PassRole` behavior in Grant a user permissions to pass a role to an AWS service.

questions.section: Content Domain 1: Data Preparation for Machine Learning (ML)
questions.question_text:
A municipal water utility's ML data engineering team receives pump telemetry in Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. The team needs to continuously cleanse records, compute short time-window aggregates, and enrich the stream before writing curated data to Amazon S3 for model training. The existing transformation logic is written in PySpark, and the team wants a managed ETL service with minimal infrastructure administration.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
questions.question_html: A municipal water utility's ML data engineering team receives pump telemetry in Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. The team needs to continuously cleanse records, compute short time-window aggregates, and enrich the stream before writing curated data to Amazon S3 for model training. The existing transformation logic is written in PySpark, and the team wants a managed ETL service with minimal infrastructure administration. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.A: Configure Amazon Data Firehose to invoke an AWS Lambda function, apply the PySpark transformations, and deliver curated output to Amazon S3.
options.B: Build an Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink application that reads from Kinesis Data Streams, rewrites the transformations with Flink APIs, and writes curated output downstream.
options.C: Create an AWS Lambda event source mapping for Kinesis Data Streams, run the aggregation logic in Lambda, and write curated batches to Amazon S3.
options.D: Create an AWS Glue streaming ETL job that reads from Kinesis Data Streams, applies the PySpark transformations, and writes curated output to Amazon S3.

options_list: Configure Amazon Data Firehose to invoke an AWS Lambda function, apply the PySpark transformations, and deliver curated output to Amazon S3.
Build an Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink application that reads from Kinesis Data Streams, rewrites the transformations with Flink APIs, and writes curated output downstream.
Create an AWS Lambda event source mapping for Kinesis Data Streams, run the aggregation logic in Lambda, and write curated batches to Amazon S3.
Create an AWS Glue streaming ETL job that reads from Kinesis Data Streams, applies the PySpark transformations, and writes curated output to Amazon S3.
correct_answers_text: Create an AWS Glue streaming ETL job that reads from Kinesis Data Streams, applies the PySpark transformations, and writes curated output to Amazon S3.
questions.explanation_text:
**AWS Glue streaming ETL** is the best fit when a team needs continuous data preparation from a streaming source and wants to use Spark-based transformations. Glue streaming jobs use the Spark streaming model, including Spark Structured Streaming micro-batches, so PySpark cleansing, enrichment, and aggregation logic can be used in a managed ETL context. See Adding streaming ETL jobs in AWS Glue and AWS Glue streaming concepts.

**Amazon Data Firehose with Lambda** is useful when the goal is to buffer, optionally transform, and deliver streaming data to destinations such as Amazon S3. That pattern is best suited to simpler record transformations before delivery, not to preserving a Spark-based ETL workflow with time-window aggregations. See Transform source data in Amazon Data Firehose.

**AWS Lambda** can consume Kinesis Data Streams records through an event source mapping and can support stateful tumbling-window processing for stream records. For this scenario, the main tradeoff is not whether Lambda can transform or aggregate records, it is whether the service matches the existing PySpark ETL approach with the least operational overhead. See Using AWS Lambda with Amazon Kinesis.

**Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink** is appropriate for custom Flink streaming applications, especially when teams want to build with Flink APIs for continuous stream processing. It is less suitable here because the team already has PySpark transformations and wants minimal rework. See Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink documentation.

questions.question_text:
A tax preparation software vendor's ML platform team manages a production Amazon SageMaker model. The team has an existing SageMaker Pipeline that retrains the model. The team needs an auditable record of SageMaker API activity, needs to monitor for a specific write operation that indicates a model promotion, and needs to start the retraining pipeline automatically with minimal custom code.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
questions.question_html: A tax preparation software vendor's ML platform team manages a production Amazon SageMaker model. The team has an existing SageMaker Pipeline that retrains the model. The team needs an auditable record of SageMaker API activity, needs to monitor for a specific write operation that indicates a model promotion, and needs to start the retraining pipeline automatically with minimal custom code. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Configure SageMaker Model Monitor quality checks, create a CloudWatch alarm for drift metrics, and invoke StartPipelineExecution on the retraining pipeline.
options.B: Enable CloudTrail data events for the training S3 bucket, query the delivered logs with Athena, and invoke StartPipelineExecution on a schedule.
options.C: Configure AWS Config rules for SageMaker endpoint resources, send noncompliance notifications to SNS, and invoke StartPipelineExecution from a subscriber.
options.D: Configure a CloudTrail trail for SageMaker management events, create an EventBridge rule for the selected API call, and invoke StartPipelineExecution on the retraining pipeline.

options_list: Configure SageMaker Model Monitor quality checks, create a CloudWatch alarm for drift metrics, and invoke StartPipelineExecution on the retraining pipeline.
Enable CloudTrail data events for the training S3 bucket, query the delivered logs with Athena, and invoke StartPipelineExecution on a schedule.
Configure AWS Config rules for SageMaker endpoint resources, send noncompliance notifications to SNS, and invoke StartPipelineExecution from a subscriber.
Configure a CloudTrail trail for SageMaker management events, create an EventBridge rule for the selected API call, and invoke StartPipelineExecution on the retraining pipeline.
correct_answers_text: Configure a CloudTrail trail for SageMaker management events, create an EventBridge rule for the selected API call, and invoke StartPipelineExecution on the retraining pipeline.
questions.explanation_text:
**CloudTrail** is the AWS service used for governance, compliance, and auditing of API activity. For SageMaker, CloudTrail records actions taken by users, roles, and AWS services, which makes it the right source when the trigger condition is a management operation such as a model promotion or endpoint-related API call. A trail can also deliver logs to Amazon S3 for longer retention and audit analysis beyond the CloudTrail event history window.

**EventBridge** is the automation layer that can react to CloudTrail API-call events. An EventBridge rule can match the relevant event pattern and call `StartPipelineExecution` to start an existing SageMaker Pipeline, which keeps the retraining workflow automated without building a polling system. SageMaker Model Monitor and CloudWatch are better suited to drift and quality thresholds, while AWS Config is better suited to configuration compliance. See AWS CloudTrail overview, Amazon SageMaker AI CloudTrail integration, EventBridge events delivered via CloudTrail, and SageMaker Pipelines with EventBridge.

questions.question_text:
A specialty pharmacy's ML operations team hosts a medication adherence prediction model on an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint. Nurses report intermittent delays during business hours. The team needs to determine whether the delays correlate with endpoint request volume or instance resource pressure. The team must use operational metrics and alarms, not audit logs or model quality reports.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
questions.question_html: A specialty pharmacy's ML operations team hosts a medication adherence prediction model on an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint. Nurses report intermittent delays during business hours. The team needs to determine whether the delays correlate with endpoint request volume or instance resource pressure. The team must use operational metrics and alarms, not audit logs or model quality reports. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Create an AWS CloudTrail trail that delivers SageMaker API activity logs to Amazon S3 for later analysis.
options.B: Create a SageMaker Model Monitor schedule to detect data quality drift and publish violation reports to Amazon S3.
options.C: Create Amazon CloudWatch dashboards and alarms for SageMaker endpoint invocations, latency, and instance utilization metrics.
options.D: Create AWS Config rules to evaluate SageMaker endpoint configuration changes and send noncompliance notifications.

options_list: Create an AWS CloudTrail trail that delivers SageMaker API activity logs to Amazon S3 for later analysis.
Create a SageMaker Model Monitor schedule to detect data quality drift and publish violation reports to Amazon S3.
Create Amazon CloudWatch dashboards and alarms for SageMaker endpoint invocations, latency, and instance utilization metrics.
Create AWS Config rules to evaluate SageMaker endpoint configuration changes and send noncompliance notifications.
correct_answers_text: Create Amazon CloudWatch dashboards and alarms for SageMaker endpoint invocations, latency, and instance utilization metrics.
questions.explanation_text:
**Amazon CloudWatch** is the primary service for operational monitoring of SageMaker infrastructure. For a real-time endpoint, the mental model is that the endpoint is a production service with traffic, latency, errors, and host-level resource pressure that must be observed over time. CloudWatch dashboards and alarms let an ML operations team correlate business-hour delays with metrics such as invocations, latency, and utilization, then notify operators or drive follow-up actions.

**SageMaker Model Monitor** addresses a different class of problem: whether production data and model behavior are drifting from expected baselines. **CloudTrail** answers audit questions such as who made an API call, while **AWS Config** answers configuration and compliance questions such as how a resource changed over time. Those services are valuable in an ML operations environment, but they do not replace CloudWatch for endpoint performance monitoring. For more information, see Monitor Amazon SageMaker with Amazon CloudWatch and Monitor workload resources.

questions.question_text:
An online grocery retailer's demand forecasting team uses a Git repository for training and inference code. A build project currently creates container images when developers merge code. The team now needs a release process that separates build automation from deployment orchestration, runs validation before any endpoint update, and prevents production changes until a reviewer approves the candidate model. The team wants managed AWS services instead of custom deployment logic in the build project.

Which TWO actions meet these requirements?
questions.question_html: An online grocery retailer's demand forecasting team uses a Git repository for training and inference code. A build project currently creates container images when developers merge code. The team now needs a release process that separates build automation from deployment orchestration, runs validation before any endpoint update, and prevents production changes until a reviewer approves the candidate model. The team wants managed AWS services instead of custom deployment logic in the build project. Which TWO actions meet these requirements?

options.A: Use SageMaker Model Monitor to approve candidate models and start endpoint deployment when drift is detected.
options.B: Use AWS CodePipeline to coordinate source, build, validation, and deployment stages, with CodeBuild used for build and test actions.
options.C: Schedule an EventBridge rule to run the training job and overwrite the endpoint configuration at fixed intervals.
options.D: Use a single CodeBuild buildspec to train the model and update the production endpoint after each successful build.
options.E: Configure the release workflow to deploy only model packages that are approved in SageMaker Model Registry.

options_list: Use SageMaker Model Monitor to approve candidate models and start endpoint deployment when drift is detected.
Use AWS CodePipeline to coordinate source, build, validation, and deployment stages, with CodeBuild used for build and test actions.
Schedule an EventBridge rule to run the training job and overwrite the endpoint configuration at fixed intervals.
Use a single CodeBuild buildspec to train the model and update the production endpoint after each successful build.
Configure the release workflow to deploy only model packages that are approved in SageMaker Model Registry.
correct_answers_text: Use AWS CodePipeline to coordinate source, build, validation, and deployment stages, with CodeBuild used for build and test actions.
Configure the release workflow to deploy only model packages that are approved in SageMaker Model Registry.
questions.explanation_text:
**CodeBuild** and **CodePipeline** solve different parts of a CI/CD workflow. CodeBuild is a managed build service that can compile code, run tests, and create artifacts. CodePipeline is the orchestration layer that connects source, build, validation, approval, and deployment stages into a controlled release process.

For ML workloads, production deployment should usually be tied to a model governance step rather than simply pushing the latest artifact. **SageMaker Model Registry** provides a managed place to track model versions and approval status, so a deployment workflow can require an approved candidate before updating an endpoint. This is especially important because a model artifact can be technically deployable but still fail model-specific validation or business review.

The common anti-pattern is to put all release behavior into a build script. That approach is simple at first, but it mixes building, testing, approval, and production deployment into one job and makes controlled promotion difficult. EventBridge and Model Monitor can participate in MLOps workflows, but they do not replace a CI/CD orchestrator and an approval gate for model releases.

For more information, see Continuous integration and continuous delivery in CodePipeline, SageMaker-provided MLOps project templates, Why use MLOps with SageMaker Projects?, and SageMaker AI workflow services.

CodePipeline is the orchestration layer that connects source, build, validation, approval, and deployment stages into a controlled release process.

For ML workloads, production deployment should usually be tied to a model governance step rather than simply pushing the latest artifact. SageMaker Model Registry provides a managed place to track model versions and approval status, so a deployment workflow can require an approved candidate before updating an endpoint. This is especially important because a model artifact can be technically deployable but still fail model-specific validation or business review.

The common anti-pattern is to put all release behavior into a build script. That approach is simple at first, but it mixes building, testing, approval, and production deployment into one job and makes controlled promotion difficult. EventBridge and Model Monitor can participate in MLOps workflows, but they do not replace a CI/CD orchestrator and an approval gate for model releases.

For more information, see Continuous integration and continuous delivery in CodePipeline, SageMaker-provided MLOps project templates, Why use MLOps with SageMaker Projects?, and SageMaker AI workflow services.

A wildlife conservation nonprofit's ML team stores millions of camera-trap images in Amazon S3. The team needs labels for an image classification training dataset. The images include confidential habitat locations, so only staff biologists are allowed to view the images. The team wants a managed labeling workflow that can reduce the amount of human labeling as labeling progresses.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

The images include confidential habitat locations, so only staff biologists are allowed to view the images. options.A: Create an Amazon A2I human review workflow, route every image, and assign a private review team.
options.B: Create one or more SageMaker Ground Truth labeling jobs, enable automated data labeling, and assign a private work team.
options.C: Create a Rekognition Custom Labels project, train from the unlabeled images, and export predicted labels.
options.D: Create Mechanical Turk HITs for the images, require confidentiality instructions, and export the completed labels.

questions.explanation_text:
**Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth** is built for creating labeled training datasets by coordinating human labeling work and storing the resulting labels for ML workflows. It supports different workforce choices, including a *private workforce*, which is the right fit when only approved employees should see the source data. Ground Truth can also use automated data labeling for supported task types, where a model learns from completed human labels and sends fewer examples to humans when confidence is high enough. For a dataset with millions of objects, the practical implementation should use multiple labeling jobs, partition the input data, or request a quota increase as needed rather than assuming the entire corpus fits into one job.

**Amazon Mechanical Turk** can be useful for public crowdsourcing, but it is not appropriate when confidential images must be restricted to internal staff. **Amazon A2I** is a human review service for ML predictions, commonly used when production predictions need oversight, not as the primary service for generating an initial labeled dataset. **Rekognition Custom Labels** can build custom image models, but it depends on labeled training images rather than solving the labeling requirement itself. For more details, see SageMaker Ground Truth overview, Create a Ground Truth labeling job, and Ground Truth workforce management.

An aerospace telemetry analytics team is standardizing deployments for Amazon SageMaker inference endpoints. A shared platform stack provisions reusable resources, including an Amazon ECR repository and networking resources. Separate model deployment stacks must provision SageMaker model and endpoint resources and use values from the shared stack. All stacks are deployed in the same AWS account and Region. The team wants consistent, repeatable provisioning through infrastructure as code and wants to avoid manual copying of resource identifiers.

Which approach will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
questions.question_html: An aerospace telemetry analytics team is standardizing deployments for Amazon SageMaker inference endpoints. A shared platform stack provisions reusable resources, including an Amazon ECR repository and networking resources. Separate model deployment stacks must provision SageMaker model and endpoint resources and use values from the shared stack. All stacks are deployed in the same AWS account and Region. The team wants consistent, repeatable provisioning through infrastructure as code and wants to avoid manual copying of resource identifiers. Which approach will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.A: Create an AWS CodeBuild project, run AWS CLI commands to create resources, and store shared values in the build logs.
options.B: Create an Amazon ECS task, provision the SageMaker resources from container code, and pass shared values as environment variables.
options.C: Create AWS CloudFormation stacks, copy shared values from the console, and paste those values into model deployment stack parameters.
options.D: Create AWS CloudFormation or AWS CDK stacks, export shared values from the platform stack, and import those values into the model deployment stacks.

options_list: Create an AWS CodeBuild project, run AWS CLI commands to create resources, and store shared values in the build logs.
Create an Amazon ECS task, provision the SageMaker resources from container code, and pass shared values as environment variables.
Create AWS CloudFormation stacks, copy shared values from the console, and paste those values into model deployment stack parameters.
Create AWS CloudFormation or AWS CDK stacks, export shared values from the platform stack, and import those values into the model deployment stacks.
correct_answers_text: Create AWS CloudFormation or AWS CDK stacks, export shared values from the platform stack, and import those values into the model deployment stacks.
questions.explanation_text:
**AWS CloudFormation** and **AWS CDK** are appropriate when an ML platform team needs repeatable provisioning rather than one-off scripts or console steps. CloudFormation models AWS resources in templates and provisions them as stacks, while CDK stacks are deployment units that synthesize to CloudFormation stacks. See the CloudFormation overview at CloudFormation overview and the CDK stack model at AWS CDK stacks guide.

For communication between stacks, the platform stack can publish identifiers such as repository names, subnet IDs, security group IDs, or endpoint-related values through `Outputs`. The model deployment stack can then consume those exported values with a cross-stack import, which avoids manually copying resource identifiers into parameters. The relevant CloudFormation mechanisms are described in CloudFormation Outputs section syntax and Fn::ImportValue reference.

The other approaches replace managed stack relationships with manual or imperative processes. CodeBuild and ECS are useful services in MLOps workflows, but they are not the best mechanism for declaring infrastructure dependencies between stacks. For SageMaker deployments, using infrastructure as code also aligns with repeatable deployment practices for resources such as `AWS::SageMaker::Model`, endpoint configurations, and endpoints.

questions.explanation_text:

When a team has already standardized on a SageMaker Pipelines workflow, the lowest-overhead deployment approach is to keep that managed workflow as the unit of automation rather than recreating the same sequence in another service.

**Infrastructure as code** tools such as AWS CloudFormation and AWS CDK support repeatable, reviewed deployments across accounts and environments. This matches the need for change control in development, staging, and production because the deployment process can promote the same declared infrastructure pattern instead of relying on manual SageMaker Studio actions.

SageMaker Projects are useful when a team wants a broader MLOps scaffold with repositories and CI/CD templates, but they are not the most direct fit when the primary need is repeatable deployment of an already standardized workflow. CodeBuild and Step Functions can participate in ML automation, but using them to reconstruct each ML step increases custom orchestration and can cause the deployed workflow to drift from the managed SageMaker Pipelines design. For more information, see Overview of Amazon SageMaker Pipelines, AWS::SageMaker::Pipeline, and AWS Step Functions integration with SageMaker.

The team needs automated unit and integration tests to run on every code change and prevent deployment when tests fail. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

An AWS CodePipeline pipeline currently builds the container image and deploys SageMaker endpoint changes. The team needs automated unit and integration tests to run on every code change and prevent deployment when tests fail. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.A: Add a SageMaker deployment guardrail before testing, shift canary traffic, and publish endpoint alarm events to CloudWatch.
options.B: Add an EventBridge rule on repository changes, invoke a Lambda test runner, and store raw test logs in Amazon S3.
options.C: Add a SageMaker Model Monitor schedule before deployment, compare captured endpoint data, and publish violations to CloudWatch.
options.D: Add a CodeBuild test action before deployment, run the suites in CodeBuild, and fail the action on test failures.

correct_answers_text: Add a CodeBuild test action before deployment, run the suites in CodeBuild, and fail the action on test failures.
questions.explanation_text:
**AWS CodePipeline** is the orchestration layer for CI/CD workflows, where changes move through stages such as source, build, test, and deploy. In this scenario, the pipeline already exists, so the lowest-overhead approach is to add a **CodeBuild** action in a test stage before the deployment stage. CodeBuild can run automated unit and integration tests as part of the pipeline, and a failed action prevents later deployment actions from running.

This pattern fits MLOps workflows in which SageMaker model code, container definitions, and pipeline definitions are versioned in a repository and promoted through an automated delivery process. Deployment guardrails and Model Monitor are useful after or during model deployment, but they do not provide a source-code test gate. EventBridge and Lambda could be assembled into a custom solution, but that would add operational overhead compared with using the existing CodePipeline and CodeBuild workflow.

For more information, see What is a pipeline in CodePipeline?, CodeBuild action reference for CodePipeline, and SageMaker Projects overview.

questions.section: Content Domain 4: ML Solution Monitoring, Maintenance, and S
questions.question_text:
A regional sports media network's personalization team hosts a video recommendation model on an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint. The team has a candidate model version and wants to evaluate whether it improves click-through rate and response latency for a limited share of live viewers. Ground truth engagement labels arrive later in the day. The team wants to compare the current and candidate models in production before increasing traffic to the candidate model. The solution must keep a single SageMaker endpoint and must not require changes to application routing logic.

Which TWO actions will meet these requirements?
questions.question_html: A regional sports media network's personalization team hosts a video recommendation model on an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint. The team has a candidate model version and wants to evaluate whether it improves click-through rate and response latency for a limited share of live viewers. Ground truth engagement labels arrive later in the day. The team wants to compare the current and candidate models in production before increasing traffic to the candidate model. The solution must keep a single SageMaker endpoint and must not require changes to application routing logic. Which TWO actions will meet these requirements?

options.A: Create a batch transform job for both models, and compare offline predictions against the next day's engagement labels.
options.B: Compare CloudWatch metrics and captured inference records by production variant before shifting more traffic to the candidate model.
options.C: Deploy the candidate model to a separate endpoint, and modify the application to randomly choose an endpoint for each request.
options.D: Send all production requests to the candidate model first, and roll back manually if CloudWatch alarms indicate degraded latency.
options.E: Configure the endpoint with the current and candidate models as production variants, and assign a small traffic weight to the candidate variant.

options_list: Create a batch transform job for both models, and compare offline predictions against the next day's engagement labels.
Compare CloudWatch metrics and captured inference records by production variant before shifting more traffic to the candidate model.
Deploy the candidate model to a separate endpoint, and modify the application to randomly choose an endpoint for each request.
Send all production requests to the candidate model first, and roll back manually if CloudWatch alarms indicate degraded latency.
Configure the endpoint with the current and candidate models as production variants, and assign a small traffic weight to the candidate variant.
correct_answers_text: Compare CloudWatch metrics and captured inference records by production variant before shifting more traffic to the candidate model.
Configure the endpoint with the current and candidate models as production variants, and assign a small traffic weight to the candidate variant.
questions.explanation_text:
**A/B testing** in Amazon SageMaker uses multiple **production variants** behind a real-time endpoint. Each variant can host a different model or instance configuration, and SageMaker can route a specified percentage of requests to each variant. This lets an ML operations team evaluate a candidate model with live traffic while keeping most users on the current model.

For monitoring, the team should use **Amazon CloudWatch** endpoint metrics and captured inference data. CloudWatch helps compare operational behavior such as traffic volume, latency, and errors across variants, while SageMaker Data Capture and Model Monitor can preserve inputs and outputs in Amazon S3 for later analysis when ground truth labels arrive. See Test models in production, Monitor Amazon SageMaker with Amazon CloudWatch, and Capture data from real-time endpoints.

Offline batch transform can be valuable for validation, but it is not a substitute for production A/B testing because it does not measure the live serving path or real viewer behavior. Creating a second endpoint and pushing randomization into the application conflicts with the stated requirement to keep routing managed by SageMaker on one endpoint. Sending all traffic to the new model first is riskier than necessary and does not satisfy the requirement to limit exposure while performance is evaluated.

questions.section: Content Domain 2: ML Model Development
questions.question_text:
A renewable energy trading desk trains an Amazon SageMaker binary classification model to predict whether wholesale electricity prices will spike the next day. The team needs a repeatable way to establish a model performance baseline before approving each new model version. Reviewers require metrics from data that was not used during training, and the same process must support comparisons against future candidate models.

Which approach will meet these requirements?
questions.question_html: A renewable energy trading desk trains an Amazon SageMaker binary classification model to predict whether wholesale electricity prices will spike the next day. The team needs a repeatable way to establish a model performance baseline before approving each new model version. Reviewers require metrics from data that was not used during training, and the same process must support comparisons against future candidate models. Which approach will meet these requirements?

options.A: Deploy each candidate model to all production traffic, collect the first day of predictions, and use those results as the approval baseline.
options.B: Add a SageMaker Pipelines evaluation step that scores a held-out test set, calculates classification metrics, and stores the metrics with the model package.
options.C: Configure the SageMaker training job to publish training accuracy to Amazon CloudWatch, and approve models when the training metric improves.
options.D: Use CloudWatch Logs Insights to query inference latency logs, and use p95 latency as the model quality baseline for approvals.

options_list: Deploy each candidate model to all production traffic, collect the first day of predictions, and use those results as the approval baseline.
Add a SageMaker Pipelines evaluation step that scores a held-out test set, calculates classification metrics, and stores the metrics with the model package.
Configure the SageMaker training job to publish training accuracy to Amazon CloudWatch, and approve models when the training metric improves.
Use CloudWatch Logs Insights to query inference latency logs, and use p95 latency as the model quality baseline for approvals.
correct_answers_text: Add a SageMaker Pipelines evaluation step that scores a held-out test set, calculates classification metrics, and stores the metrics with the model package.
questions.explanation_text:
A practical **model performance baseline** should measure how well a trained model performs on data that was not used to fit the model. For a binary classifier, relevant baseline metrics commonly include precision, recall, F1 score, and accuracy, depending on the business tradeoff. In SageMaker, a repeatable pattern is to place evaluation into an automated workflow, such as a SageMaker Pipelines step, and store the resulting metrics with the model artifact or model package so future versions can be compared consistently.

Training metrics emitted during the training job can help diagnose convergence or overfitting, but they are not a substitute for an evaluation baseline on unseen data. Production variants and A/B testing are valuable for online validation, but they usually come after a candidate has passed offline evaluation. Model Monitor can later use model quality baselines and ground-truth labels to detect drift in production, but the baseline still depends on meaningful predictions and labels. For more information, see Model validation in Amazon SageMaker, Monitor and analyze training jobs using Amazon CloudWatch metrics, and Create a model quality baseline.

questions.section: Content Domain 1: Data Preparation for Machine Learning (ML)
questions.question_text:
An international hotel group's loyalty analytics team is preparing an ML training dataset from guest profiles, reservation history, and free-text service notes that are stored in Amazon S3. The raw data contains names, email addresses, phone numbers, loyalty identifiers, and special request notes. Compliance requires the team to find sensitive data in the S3 data lake, prevent raw PII from being included in the training dataset, and store the curated training output only in the approved AWS Region.

Which combination of steps should the team take? (Select TWO.)
questions.question_html: An international hotel group's loyalty analytics team is preparing an ML training dataset from guest profiles, reservation history, and free-text service notes that are stored in Amazon S3. The raw data contains names, email addresses, phone numbers, loyalty identifiers, and special request notes. Compliance requires the team to find sensitive data in the S3 data lake, prevent raw PII from being included in the training dataset, and store the curated training output only in the approved AWS Region. Which combination of steps should the team take? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Run Amazon Macie discovery jobs on the S3 buckets to identify objects that contain sensitive data.
options.B: Use Amazon Athena views to hide sensitive columns while allowing the training job to read the original S3 objects.
options.C: Register trained model versions in Amazon SageMaker Model Registry after the training workflow completes.
options.D: Replicate the raw S3 objects to buckets in multiple Regions before running the data preparation workflow.
options.E: Apply AWS Glue DataBrew PII transformations to mask or delete sensitive fields and write the output to S3 in the approved Region.

options_list: Run Amazon Macie discovery jobs on the S3 buckets to identify objects that contain sensitive data.
Use Amazon Athena views to hide sensitive columns while allowing the training job to read the original S3 objects.
Register trained model versions in Amazon SageMaker Model Registry after the training workflow completes.
Replicate the raw S3 objects to buckets in multiple Regions before running the data preparation workflow.
Apply AWS Glue DataBrew PII transformations to mask or delete sensitive fields and write the output to S3 in the approved Region.
correct_answers_text: Run Amazon Macie discovery jobs on the S3 buckets to identify objects that contain sensitive data.
Apply AWS Glue DataBrew PII transformations to mask or delete sensitive fields and write the output to S3 in the approved Region.
questions.explanation_text:
For ML data preparation under compliance constraints, separate the problem into two controls: **discover where sensitive data exists** and **produce a sanitized training dataset**. Amazon Macie is appropriate for discovering sensitive data in Amazon S3, including common PII patterns, so the team can identify risky buckets and objects before feature engineering begins. See Amazon Macie managed data identifiers.

After discovery, the team still needs to transform the data. AWS Glue DataBrew is a visual data preparation tool that can profile datasets and apply PII-oriented transformations such as masking, hashing, encryption, nulling, or deletion. The curated result should be written to S3 only in the approved AWS Region so downstream training jobs use the sanitized data rather than the raw source records. The related AWS Glue sensitive data capabilities are described in Detect and process sensitive data in AWS Glue.

A common anti-pattern is to rely only on query-time filtering while leaving training pipelines pointed at raw data. That might reduce what some users see in one query path, but it does not create a clean ML training artifact and can lead to accidental leakage through another consumer. Similarly, copying raw PII into additional Regions before transformation increases compliance risk and directly works against a data residency requirement.

questions.question_text:
A biomedical device manufacturer's quality analytics team prepares monthly ML training extracts from a relational quality system. Each extract is a small tabular file that quality engineers review in spreadsheet tools before the file is loaded into Amazon S3 for downstream experiments. The team values simple interchange with non-engineering users and does not need to optimize large analytical scans.

Which data format should the team use for these extracts?
questions.question_html: A biomedical device manufacturer's quality analytics team prepares monthly ML training extracts from a relational quality system. Each extract is a small tabular file that quality engineers review in spreadsheet tools before the file is loaded into Amazon S3 for downstream experiments. The team values simple interchange with non-engineering users and does not need to optimize large analytical scans. Which data format should the team use for these extracts?

options.A: Write the monthly extracts as CSV files with consistent column names and delimiters.
options.B: Write the monthly extracts as ORC files with columnar storage for analytics.
options.C: Write the monthly extracts as JSON files with one nested object per record.
options.D: Write the monthly extracts as Parquet files with columnar encoding and compression.

options_list: Write the monthly extracts as CSV files with consistent column names and delimiters.
Write the monthly extracts as ORC files with columnar storage for analytics.
Write the monthly extracts as JSON files with one nested object per record.
Write the monthly extracts as Parquet files with columnar encoding and compression.
correct_answers_text: Write the monthly extracts as CSV files with consistent column names and delimiters.
questions.explanation_text:
For data preparation, the best format depends on the **access pattern**, not on a single universally best storage choice. CSV is a practical choice for small, fixed-schema tabular data that people need to inspect, exchange, or edit with common tools. It is human readable and widely supported, which reduces friction when non-engineering users participate in data review.

Columnar formats such as **Parquet** and **ORC** are often better for large analytical datasets because engines can read selected columns efficiently and reduce scanned data. That tradeoff matters for workloads such as Amazon Athena or Redshift Spectrum queries over large S3 datasets, but it is not the priority in this scenario. AWS documents these columnar-format benefits in Amazon Athena guidance on when to use columnar formats such as Parquet and ORC, and AWS Glue lists supported ETL formats, including CSV, JSON, Parquet, and ORC, in AWS Glue documentation for ETL input and output data formats.

questions.section: Content Domain 2: ML Model Development
questions.question_text:
A public transit authority's analytics team trains a neural network in Amazon SageMaker to predict whether a bus route will miss its on-time target. The model reaches high accuracy on the training dataset, but its accuracy is much lower on a held-out validation dataset. The team wants to improve performance on new route data without collecting additional data or adding new features.

Which action should the ML engineer take?
questions.question_html: A public transit authority's analytics team trains a neural network in Amazon SageMaker to predict whether a bus route will miss its on-time target. The model reaches high accuracy on the training dataset, but its accuracy is much lower on a held-out validation dataset. The team wants to improve performance on new route data without collecting additional data or adding new features. Which action should the ML engineer take?

options.A: Reduce dropout in the network and decrease L2 weight decay during retraining.
options.B: Optimize only for training accuracy and select the run with the highest score.
options.C: Add more hidden layers to the network and increase the number of epochs.
options.D: Increase dropout in the network and tune L2 weight decay during retraining.

options_list: Reduce dropout in the network and decrease L2 weight decay during retraining.
Optimize only for training accuracy and select the run with the highest score.
Add more hidden layers to the network and increase the number of epochs.
Increase dropout in the network and tune L2 weight decay during retraining.
correct_answers_text: Increase dropout in the network and tune L2 weight decay during retraining.
questions.explanation_text:
When a model performs much better on training data than on held-out validation data, the practical concern is **overfitting**. Regularization techniques deliberately constrain the model so it is less likely to learn noise or accidental patterns in the training set.

**Dropout** randomly disables a fraction of neural network units during training, which discourages codependent behavior among neurons. **L2 regularization**, often implemented as weight decay, penalizes large weights and tends to produce smoother models that generalize better.

Adding layers or training for more epochs increases model capacity or training exposure, which can worsen overfitting if no additional controls are applied. Optimizing only for training accuracy is also risky because the goal is not memorization, it is performance on unseen data.

The AWS exam guide explicitly includes the AWS Certified Machine Learning Engineer - Associate Domain 2 outline skill area for regularization techniques. AWS documentation also describes regularization as a way to address overfitting in Model Fit: Underfitting vs. Overfitting, and documents SageMaker examples such as dropout in Object2Vec Hyperparameters and `wd` as weight decay in Linear Learner Hyperparameters.

questions.question_text:
An automotive warranty analytics team hosts a fraud risk model on an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint. The team has baseline statistics from the training dataset, but confirmed fraud labels can take several weeks to arrive. The team wants daily alerts when production request features show distribution shifts, missing or unexpected features, or unusual values before labels are available. The solution must require the least custom monitoring code.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
questions.question_html: An automotive warranty analytics team hosts a fraud risk model on an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint. The team has baseline statistics from the training dataset, but confirmed fraud labels can take several weeks to arrive. The team wants daily alerts when production request features show distribution shifts, missing or unexpected features, or unusual values before labels are available. The solution must require the least custom monitoring code. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Enable Data Capture, configure model quality checks only, and publish accuracy metrics to CloudWatch alarms each day.
options.B: Enable Data Capture, create a baseline from the training dataset, and schedule SageMaker Model Monitor data quality checks with CloudWatch alarms.
options.C: Analyze CloudTrail management events for the SageMaker endpoint and trigger EventBridge notifications for unusual write activity.
options.D: Create CloudWatch dashboards for endpoint invocations, latency, CPU, and memory, and alarm on abnormal endpoint utilization.

options_list: Enable Data Capture, configure model quality checks only, and publish accuracy metrics to CloudWatch alarms each day.
Enable Data Capture, create a baseline from the training dataset, and schedule SageMaker Model Monitor data quality checks with CloudWatch alarms.
Analyze CloudTrail management events for the SageMaker endpoint and trigger EventBridge notifications for unusual write activity.
Create CloudWatch dashboards for endpoint invocations, latency, CPU, and memory, and alarm on abnormal endpoint utilization.
correct_answers_text: Enable Data Capture, create a baseline from the training dataset, and schedule SageMaker Model Monitor data quality checks with CloudWatch alarms.
questions.explanation_text:
**SageMaker Model Monitor** is designed to monitor deployed models by running scheduled monitoring jobs against captured inference data. For this scenario, the key constraint is that labels are not available for weeks, so the practical first signal is whether live input data still resembles the training baseline. Data quality monitoring compares production features with baseline statistics and constraints, then emits metrics that can be used with CloudWatch alarms.

**Data Capture** records inference inputs and outputs from a SageMaker endpoint to Amazon S3, which gives monitoring jobs data to analyze without adding custom logging code to the application. This captured data can also support debugging and later retraining workflows. See Capture data from real-time endpoints and Monitor data quality.

Model quality monitoring is valuable when ground truth labels are available because it can track performance metrics such as accuracy-related measures for classification or regression metrics for regression workloads. However, it is not the best answer when the requirement is to detect problems *before* delayed labels arrive. CloudWatch endpoint metrics and CloudTrail events remain important for operations and auditing, but they do not inspect the statistical quality of model input features. For a broader view of monitoring types, see Monitor models for data and model quality, bias, and feature attribution drift.

questions.section: Content Domain 2: ML Model Development
questions.question_text:
A municipal tax agency's compliance analytics team is building a binary classification model in Amazon SageMaker AI to flag filings for possible audit. The dataset is tabular, labeled, normalized, and shuffled. The agency must catch at least a specified percentage of truly noncompliant filings, but within that constraint wants to reduce the number of compliant filings sent to audit. The team wants to use a SageMaker AI built-in algorithm with minimal custom code.

Which approach should the team use?
questions.question_html: A municipal tax agency's compliance analytics team is building a binary classification model in Amazon SageMaker AI to flag filings for possible audit. The dataset is tabular, labeled, normalized, and shuffled. The agency must catch at least a specified percentage of truly noncompliant filings, but within that constraint wants to reduce the number of compliant filings sent to audit. The team wants to use a SageMaker AI built-in algorithm with minimal custom code. Which approach should the team use?

options.A: Train a SageMaker AI K-Means model, set the number of clusters to two, and label the higher-risk cluster as the audit class.
options.B: Train a SageMaker AI Linear Learner binary classifier, set the model selection criteria to precision at target recall, and configure the required target recall.
options.C: Train a SageMaker AI XGBoost model, set the evaluation metric to RMSE, and select the training job with the lowest validation error.
options.D: Train a SageMaker AI Linear Learner binary classifier, set the model selection criteria to recall at target precision, and configure the audit precision target.

options_list: Train a SageMaker AI K-Means model, set the number of clusters to two, and label the higher-risk cluster as the audit class.
Train a SageMaker AI Linear Learner binary classifier, set the model selection criteria to precision at target recall, and configure the required target recall.
Train a SageMaker AI XGBoost model, set the evaluation metric to RMSE, and select the training job with the lowest validation error.
Train a SageMaker AI Linear Learner binary classifier, set the model selection criteria to recall at target precision, and configure the audit precision target.
correct_answers_text: Train a SageMaker AI Linear Learner binary classifier, set the model selection criteria to precision at target recall, and configure the required target recall.
questions.explanation_text:
**Recall** measures how many actual positive cases the model catches, so it is the right constraint when missing a positive case is the more serious failure. In this scenario, the positive class is a truly noncompliant filing, and the agency must catch at least a specified percentage of those cases. Once that recall requirement is met, improving **precision** reduces the number of compliant filings incorrectly sent to audit.

For a labeled tabular binary classification problem, SageMaker AI built-in algorithms can reduce implementation effort because the team can use managed training rather than maintaining its own algorithm container. **Linear Learner** is suitable when the team wants a built-in supervised algorithm for regression or classification and the data has already been prepared appropriately. Its target recall and target precision settings are designed for this kind of practical model-selection tradeoff, where the business requirement is not simply highest overall accuracy.

The opposite Linear Learner setting would optimize recall while holding precision fixed, which is not the same operational requirement. XGBoost is also a common SageMaker AI algorithm for tabular data, but choosing RMSE does not express the recall constraint. K-Means is plausible only if the team lacked labels and wanted exploratory clustering, but this scenario has labels and needs supervised binary classification behavior.

For more about SageMaker AI algorithm choices and training options, see Use Amazon SageMaker built-in algorithms or pre-trained models and Train a model with Amazon SageMaker.

questions.question_text:
A national grocery chain's demand forecasting team manages Amazon SageMaker Pipelines definitions and inference container code in a GitHub repository. The team has standardized on GitHub Flow: short-lived feature branches, pull requests, and a main branch that is always deployable. The team wants merges into main to automatically build and test the container image, run the SageMaker model build pipeline, and start the deployment workflow. The team wants to use managed AWS CI/CD services with the least custom orchestration.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
questions.question_html: A national grocery chain's demand forecasting team manages Amazon SageMaker Pipelines definitions and inference container code in a GitHub repository. The team has standardized on GitHub Flow: short-lived feature branches, pull requests, and a main branch that is always deployable. The team wants merges into main to automatically build and test the container image, run the SageMaker model build pipeline, and start the deployment workflow. The team wants to use managed AWS CI/CD services with the least custom orchestration. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.A: Create a SageMaker Project with CodePipeline connected to GitHub, trigger the pipeline on pushes to develop, and merge develop into main after the deployment workflow.
options.B: Create a SageMaker Project with CodePipeline connected to GitHub, trigger the pipeline on pushes to main, and run CodeBuild steps for the SageMaker build and deployment workflow.
options.C: Create a Lambda function to poll GitHub pull requests continuously, and invoke CodeDeploy directly when a pull request is opened against main.
options.D: Create an EventBridge scheduled rule to start the SageMaker Pipeline hourly, and configure the pipeline to pull the latest main branch commit during execution.

options_list: Create a SageMaker Project with CodePipeline connected to GitHub, trigger the pipeline on pushes to develop, and merge develop into main after the deployment workflow.
Create a SageMaker Project with CodePipeline connected to GitHub, trigger the pipeline on pushes to main, and run CodeBuild steps for the SageMaker build and deployment workflow.
Create a Lambda function to poll GitHub pull requests continuously, and invoke CodeDeploy directly when a pull request is opened against main.
Create an EventBridge scheduled rule to start the SageMaker Pipeline hourly, and configure the pipeline to pull the latest main branch commit during execution.
correct_answers_text: Create a SageMaker Project with CodePipeline connected to GitHub, trigger the pipeline on pushes to main, and run CodeBuild steps for the SageMaker build and deployment workflow.
questions.explanation_text:
**GitHub Flow** treats `main` as the deployable branch, so the automation should be tied to changes that land on `main`, not to a separate long-lived integration branch. In an AWS ML workflow, **SageMaker Projects** can provide the MLOps scaffolding around source control, model build pipelines, model registry usage, and deployment automation.

**CodePipeline** is the managed orchestration layer for a sequence such as source, build, test, provision, and deploy. A source connection to GitHub can start a pipeline from repository events, and branch filters let the team align the trigger with the selected branching strategy. See GitHub connections and pipeline triggers.

Using a `develop` branch would be more consistent with Gitflow, not the stated GitHub Flow process. Using a schedule or a custom polling Lambda function separates deployment from the actual Git event, adds custom orchestration, and can make traceability from commit to pipeline run less direct. For more context on branch patterns, see Git branching strategies and SageMaker Projects.

questions.question_text:
A satellite imagery startup's ML team has a custom PyTorch training script that trains a convolutional neural network. The team wants to run the training job on Amazon SageMaker AI managed training infrastructure. The team wants to use a SageMaker AI supported framework container and avoid maintaining a custom Docker image. The training data is stored in Amazon S3, and the trained model artifacts must be available in Amazon S3 after training.

Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)
questions.question_html: A satellite imagery startup's ML team has a custom PyTorch training script that trains a convolutional neural network. The team wants to run the training job on Amazon SageMaker AI managed training infrastructure. The team wants to use a SageMaker AI supported framework container and avoid maintaining a custom Docker image. The training data is stored in Amazon S3, and the trained model artifacts must be available in Amazon S3 after training. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

options.A: Create a SageMaker AI PyTorch estimator that specifies the training script as the entry point.
options.B: Configure the training job to read input channels from Amazon S3 and write model output to Amazon S3.
options.C: Build a custom Docker image that includes PyTorch, the training script, and all runtime dependencies.
options.D: Select the SageMaker AI Linear Learner built-in algorithm and provide the PyTorch script as a training parameter.
options.E: Run the PyTorch script on an Amazon EC2 instance and copy the completed model artifacts into Amazon S3.

options_list: Create a SageMaker AI PyTorch estimator that specifies the training script as the entry point.
Configure the training job to read input channels from Amazon S3 and write model output to Amazon S3.
Build a custom Docker image that includes PyTorch, the training script, and all runtime dependencies.
Select the SageMaker AI Linear Learner built-in algorithm and provide the PyTorch script as a training parameter.
Run the PyTorch script on an Amazon EC2 instance and copy the completed model artifacts into Amazon S3.
correct_answers_text: Create a SageMaker AI PyTorch estimator that specifies the training script as the entry point.
Configure the training job to read input channels from Amazon S3 and write model output to Amazon S3.
questions.explanation_text:
**SageMaker AI script mode** is designed for cases where you have custom training code, such as a `.py` script, but do not want to build an entire container yourself. You use a SageMaker supported framework estimator, such as PyTorch or TensorFlow, and provide an `entry_point` script. SageMaker supplies the prebuilt framework container and manages the training job infrastructure.

In a managed SageMaker training workflow, training data is typically stored in **Amazon S3**, and the training job writes model artifacts back to S3 when training completes. This separates the code, compute, input data, and output artifacts cleanly, which is why SageMaker can spin up training resources for the job and tear them down afterward.

Building a custom Docker image is useful when the built-in framework containers do not meet your needs, but it is unnecessary overhead in this scenario. Built-in algorithms are also not the right fit because they are prepackaged algorithm implementations, not a way to run arbitrary PyTorch code. Running training manually on Amazon EC2 is a valid general compute pattern, but it gives up the managed training lifecycle that SageMaker provides.

For more information, see Use machine learning algorithms in Amazon SageMaker AI, Use PyTorch with Amazon SageMaker AI, and Use Docker containers with SageMaker AI.
